Anaphylaxis is a dangerous allergic reaction that occurs quickly and can cause death.
Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency that may require immediate medical attention such as airway management, supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids, and intensive care.
Anaphylaxis can occur in response to any abnormality.
Anaphylaxis to penicillin occurs once in 2,000 to 10,000 cases per treatment, and death occurs in less than one in 50,000 cases per treatment.

CHAPTER ten Perhaps there is nothing more delightful in the romance of boyhood than the finding of some secret hiding place whither a body may creep away from the bustle of the world's life, to nestle in quietness for an hour or two.
More especially is such delightful.
One may look down upon the bustling matters of busy every day life, while one lies snugly hidden away unseen by any, as though one were in some strange invisible world of one's own.
Myles and Gascoyne found one summer afternoon.
They called it their Eyry, and the name suited well for the roosting place of the young hawks that rested in its windy stillness, looking down upon the shifting castle life in the courts below.
Behind the north stable.
A great, long, rambling building, thick walled, and black with age, lay an older part of the castle than that peopled by the better class of life a cluster of great thick walls, rudely but strongly built, now the dwelling place of stable lads and hinds.
Swine and poultry.
From one part of these ancient walls, and fronting an inner court of the castle, arose a tall, circular, heavy buttressed tower, considerably higher than the other buildings, and so mantled with a dense growth of aged ivy.
As to stand a shaft of solid green.
Above its crumbling crown circled hundreds of pigeons, white and pied, clapping and clattering in noisy flight through the sunny air.
Several windows, some closed with shutters.
And near the top of the pile was a row of arched openings, as though of a balcony or an airy gallery.
Myles had more than once felt an idle curiosity about this tower, and one day, as he and Gascoyne sat together.
He pointed his finger and said, What is yon place? That, answered Gascoyne.
Telleth me that there be stairways built in the wall and passage ways, and a maze wherein a body may get lost, an he know not the way aright, and never see the blessed light of day again.
Marry, said Myles.
Who liveth there now? No one liveth there, said Gascoyne, saving only some of the stable villains, and that half witted goose herd who flung stones at us yesterday when we mocked him down in the paddock.
He and his wife and those others dwell in the vaults beneath.
Like rabbits in any warren.
No one else hath lived there since Earl Robert's day.
The story goeth that Earl Robert's brother or step brother was murdered there, and some men say by the Earl himself.
Sin that day it hath been tight shut.
Myles stared at the tower for a while in silence.
It is a strange seeming place from without, said he, at last, and mayhap it may be even more strange inside.
Hast ever been within, Francis? Nay, said Gascoyne.
An I had lived here in this place so long as thou, I wot I would have been within it ere this.

Whoever has read the tale of the Hind and Panther with attention.
Must have perceived that, while that work was in progress, a great alteration took place in the views of those who used Dryden as their interpreter.
At first the Church of England is mentioned with tenderness and respect, and is exhorted.
To ally herself with the Roman Catholics against the Puritan sects but at the close of the poem.
With the Roman Catholics against the Church of England.
This change in the language of the court poet was indicative of a great change in the policy of the court.
The original purpose of James had been to obtain for the Church of which he was a member.
At the Council board, while Massey held a deanery.
Which had been entrusted to his care.
Such had been his policy as long as he could cherish, any hope that the Church of England would consent to share ascendency with the Church of Rome.
That hope at one time amounted to confidence.
The enthusiasm with which the Tories had hailed his accession, the elections, the dutiful language and ample grants of his Parliament.
He felt an assurance that every obstacle would give way before his power and his resolution.
His Parliament withstood him.
He tried the effects of frowns and menaces.
Frowns and menaces failed.
He tried the effect of prorogation.
From the day of the prorogation the opposition to his designs had been growing stronger and stronger.
He must effect it in defiance of that great party which had given such signal proofs of fidelity to his office, to his family, and to his person.
The whole Anglican priesthood, the whole Cavalier gentry, were against him.
In vain had he, by virtue of his ecclesiastical supremacy, enjoined the clergy to abstain from discussing controverted points.
Every parish in the nation.

As Myles took his place at the south end of the lists, he found the Sieur de la Montaigne already at his station.
Through the peep hole in the face of the huge helmet, a transverse slit known as the occularium, he could see, like a strange narrow picture.
The sunlight gleaming and flashing upon his polished plates of steel, and the trappings of his horse swaying and fluttering in the rushing of the fresh breeze.
Upon that motionless figure his sight gradually centred with every faculty of mind and soul.
He ground his teeth together with stern resolve to do his best in the coming encounter, and murmured a brief prayer in the hallow darkness of his huge helm.
Slowly raised his spear point until the shaft reached the exact angle, and there suffered it to rest motionless.
There was a moment of dead, tense, breathless pause, then he rather felt than saw the Marshal raise his baton.
He gathered himself together.

CORRELATED VARIATION.
In man, as in the lower animals, many structures are so intimately related, that when one part varies so does another.
Without our being able, in most cases, to assign any reason.
We cannot say whether the one part governs the other, or whether both are governed by some earlier developed part.
Various monstrosities, as I.
Geoffroy repeatedly insists.
Are thus intimately connected.
Homologous structures are particularly liable to change together, as we see on the opposite sides of the body.

Like the lion, however, it was more frightened than we, and charged away from us through the jungle.

A most hopeless, terrible place should one be lost in it, with certain death either by thirst or by savage beasts staring one in the face.
Clearly, then, the only thing to do was to return to the river and in order to accomplish this before dark it was necessary that no time should be lost.

The tireless Mahina had also collected some dry grass for my bed, and I turned in at once, with my rifle handy, and slept the sleep of the just, regardless of all the wild beasts in Africa.
At dawn Mabruki roused me with a cup of steaming hot coffee and some biscuits, and a start was at once made on our return journey to Tsavo.
The place where we had struck the Sabaki the previous evening.

As we made our way up the Sabaki, we discovered a beautiful waterfall about a hundred and fifty feet high not a sheer drop, but a series of cascades.

And which he bought for seven gold pieces.
Now it happened that there were three merry rascals hanging about the market place, who much preferred living on other people's goods to working for their own living.

But how shall we manage it, ' asked one of them.

If we only stick to it you'll see the mule will soon be ours'.
This proposal quite satisfied the others, and they all separated as they had agreed.

Where have you been'? asked the thief.
To the market, ' was the reply.

This mule.
The one I'm sitting upon, to be sure, ' replied Simon.

A donkey? Rubbish' screamed Simon.

Our analysis suggests that improving case management should be a tool to reduce transmission and prevalence in both low and high endemic areas.
Indeed, when in low endemic areas Fig.
four Moderate incidence reduction following an increase of case management to sixty percent coverage in Kenya, Mozambique, and Benin.
(A) Incidence and incidence reduction after increase of effective treatment to sixty percent.

Countries where current case management coverage is lowest should be prioritized given the biggest need and biggest impact predicted in this context.
The effect of treatment of uncomplicated malaria cases on transmission and burden may be several fold.
Our results align with previously published modeling work.
For example, Okell et al.
Demonstrated a significant role of ACTs in transmission reduction strategies, especially in lower tranmission settings [forty-four].
Increasing effective access to care through greater health systems performance can be tackled at different levels in the cascade of care [seven, forty-nine].
WHO recommends early diagnosis and treatment for effective case management [four].
Finally, in order to maximise the drug’s efficacy, parasite resistance to drugs needs to be monitored and addressed rapidly if it arises [fifty-six].
The current estimates show that the highest estimate of effective treatment was found in Uganda, of sixty-one percent.
OpenMalaria has been previously developed and is discussed in detail elsewhere [nineteen], but the model has some limitations relevant to this work.
The model was mainly fitted to cross sectional surveys, limiting the certainty on implemented parasite dynamics.
The absence of longitudinal data of malaria infections in endemic areas makes it challenging to accurately model immune dynamics.
As such, estimates of population level severe incidence remain uncertain.
Simulations focus on the effect of increasing effective treatment of symptomatic malaria cases across the population.

This study investigates the prevalence of dissemination- and outcome reporting biases in registered interventional malaria research.
Methods All malaria interventional trials registered on ClinicalTrials.
Gov from twenty ten to twenty twenty were identified.
Subsequently, publications that matched the registration were searched.
Results A total of five hundred seventy-nine trials were identified on ClinicalTrials.
Gov, of which five hundred forty-four met the inclusion criteria.
six percent of these trials (one hundred ninety-nine/five hundred forty-four) were registered retrospectively, with one hundred twenty-nine (twenty-three point seven  percent).
seven percent registered after the first patient enrolment and seventy (twelve point nine  percent).
nine percent following study completion.
Publications were identified for three hundred fifty-one out of five hundred forty-four registered trials (sixty-four point five  percent).
five percent, involving one million, five hundred twenty-six thousand eighty-one study participants.
Conversely, publications were not found for one hundred ninety-three of the five hundred forty-four registrations (thirty-five point five  percent).
five percent, which aimed to enrol four hundred seventeen thousand, nine hundred twenty-two study participants.
Among these five hundred forty-four registrations, four hundred forty-four (eighty-one point zero  percent).

six percent (two hundred twenty-two/four hundred sixty-six) of the published trials, and an even higher discordance rate of seventy-three point two  percent.

Be Full list of author information is available at the end of the articlePool et al.
There is a growing recognition of the importance of transparently sharing research results both timely and comprehensively [seven, eight, thirteen, fourteen].
Adhering to best practices in study registration and reporting is essential for advancing evidence-based medicine [nineteen, twenty].
Additionally, some argue that evidence-based medicine is compromised due to biased trials and selective publication driven by industry funding [twenty-four].
This study aims to investigate the magnitude of biases within the field of malaria research.
STROBE reporting guidelines for cross-sectional studies were followed [twenty-five] (see STROBE checklist in Keywords Malaria research trials, ClinicalTrials.
Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
This study is an observational cross-sectional study of malaria trials registered on www.creativecommons.org.
Gov, a major database of clinical studies conducted around the world [twenty-six].
This study did not receive internal or external funding [twenty-seven].
Only interventional malaria trials were eligible.
Interventional trials, as defined by ClinicalTrials.
The group assignments are determined by the study protocol, and participants may receive diagnostic, therapeutic, or other forms of intervention.
Data were downloaded on November fifteen, twenty twenty-two.
A completion date of July one, twenty twenty-one, was set to allow enough time for the publication of the registered trials.
Publications corresponding to trials registered on ClinicalTrials.
The searches also included checks for results posted on ClinicalTrials.
Gov, and were last updated on January twenty-four, twenty twenty-four, using tools such as ChatGPTfour and Perplexity.
Online preprint servers such as medRxiv were not included in the search.
Full texts of search results were reviewed to assess their association with an NCT registration.
If no response was received after the initial contact, two additional follow-up emails were sent at intervals of seven–ten days.
Trials that received no response were classified as unpublished.
Additional details, including the identification of subsequent publications and analysis of publication bias, are provided in Supplementary File one.
Registrations were downloaded from ClinicalTrials.
The number of enrolled participants and the time from study completion to publication were calculated.
The median time from trial completion to publication was initially calculated for the first publication per registered trial (online first date).
For four registrations, there was no completion date; in those four cases, the ClinicalTrials.
Gov registered ‘primary completion date’ was used as alternative.
Further details on variables and analyses are available in Supplementary file one.
If a single NCT number corresponded to one or more publications, all relevant publications were included in the outcome reporting bias analysis.

Of the five hundred forty-four trial registrations, three hundred eighty-two (seventy percent) led to a total of five hundred seventy-four ‘reporting events’ (dissemination in any form).

Molecular diagnosis by PCR identified Plasmodium relictum, lineage GRWeleven as the aetiological agent.
The bird presented died most likely due to an acute infection as evidenced by the high blood parasitaemia, leading to major erythrocyte destruction.
Further analyses of feral pigeons (n = twenty-two) did not reveal any additional cases of Plasmodium infections.
Conclusion This study reports the first mortality associated with P. falciparum.
Relictum lineage GRWeleven.
The study supports previous studies, suggesting that Plasmodium infections are not frequent in pigeons.
Host conditions like immunosuppression due to the tumour may have influenced the infection outcome in this fatal case.
Use of anti-P. falciparum HSPseventy antibody for detection of P.
Relictum antigens for immune assays in blood and tissue samples will be a useful tool for future studies.

However, some bird species have adapted to live in close proximity to humans in urban and periurban areas.
Problems include noise pollution, deterioration of architectonic and urban heritage through soiling with their droppings and disease transmission [four].
Feral pigeons are known for carrying various pathogens, some of which are zoonotic such as Chlamydia psittaci, Salmonella spp.
Cryptococcus neoformans and the parasite Toxoplasma gondii [five–seven].
Haemosporidia are also common parasites infecting pigeons, namely protozoans in the genera Haemoproteus, Leucocytozoon and Plasmodium.

Parasitology tests Microscopic examination of Hemacolor rapid-stained impression smears revealed an asynchronous infection of haemoparasites (Fig. two).
Round and irregularly shaped trophozoites were seen and mature trophozoites displaced the host erythrocyte nucleus.
Erythrocytic meronts containing up to eighteen merozoites, with characteristic clumped-up haemozoin pigment were seen.
Round gametocytes with scattered haemozoin pigment were present in the blood film and most displaced the host erythrocyte nucleus (Fig. three).
The parasitaemia was determined to be approximately eighteen percent.

The antibody staining was diffusely distributed in the parasite cytoplasm.

Follow‑up The other pigeons of the owner were reported to be in good health.
The owner was advised to isolate wild/feral birds and test them before mixing with his pets.
Adoption of wild birds is not advised unless approved by veterinary authorities.
Wild birds may harbour diseases that are transmitted to pets and/or to humans.
It is also unadvisable to move birds between geographical borders, as this may spread diseases between regions.
In January twenty twenty-four, another dead pigeon was submitted to the NRGK by the same owner.
Upon necropsy, the bird was emaciated.
The gizzard contained two broken paperclips.

Discussion This case describes avian malaria infection in a feral-pet pigeon, as confirmed by an extensive diagnostic work-up.
This is the first time this lineage has been reported in a pigeon (Columbiformes).
Information on the pathogenicity of this lineage in natural infections is lacking.
Experimental infections of GRWeleven in canaries have reported mild infection with low parasitaemia during the acute phase, in contrast to P. falciparum.
Relictum SGSone which is known to cause high parasitaemia in canaries [thirty-seven].
In the case presented here, the pigeon infected with P. knowlesi.
Relictum GRWeleven had high parasitaemia and evidently all erythrocytic stages of the parasite were present.
When the rate of erythropoiesis cannot compensate for the erythrocyte loss through destruction, anaemia is inevitable [thirty-eight].
Hill CM [thirty-nine] reported severe anaemia due to reduced number of erythrocytes as a proximate cause of death in pigeons infected with P. knowlesi.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
These changes are often seen in avian malaria infections [forty].
Infection with Plasmodium triggers inflammatory infiltrates of leukocytes.
Monocytes, lymphocytes or heterophils), and these were noted in various organs [forty-one, forty-two].
This has been reported in previous studies with avian, human, and rodent malaria infections [twenty-six, forty-three].
This factor may have contributed to the bird succumbing to infection.
Exoerythrocytic meronts (phanerozoites) were not seen in the examined organs.
These parasitic forms are mostly known to originate from natural or sporozoite inoculated infections [twenty-eight].
Phanerozoites may be differentiated from the phagocytosed erythrocytic meronts that we observed in this study by their lack of haemozoin pigment.
Relictum infections, exoerythrocytic meronts are limited once the blood infection is established [twenty-eight, forty-four].
Recent publications have reported the absence of phanerozoites in P. ovale.
Relictum infections in wild and experimental birds and some authors suggest that some strains of P. knowlesi.
Relictum may not develop phanerozoites altogether [twenty, thirty-seven, forty-five].
In canaries, phanerozoites were observed in endothelial cells of brain capillaries [thirty-eight].
However, in a more recent study, these parasite stages were not detected in experimentally infected canaries [forty-five].
Farmer JN and Moore AK [forty-six] reported death in ten out of thirty-eight P. knowlesi.
Relictum experimentally infected pigeons during the course of infection.
In four of the ten dead birds, phanerozoites were observed mostly in the brain and some in the liver and spleen.
In another study on P. malariae.
Relictum-infected puffins, phanerozoites have been observed in two out of three infected birds, in the liver, spleen, kidney, lung and heart [twenty-six].
These studies suggest that the development of exoerythrocytic parasite forms may be dependent on the parasite strain and/or the avian host infected.
The physiological state of the host during infection plays a major role in determining infection outcome.
For example, hosts in poor health may be predisposed to infectious diseases due to immunodeficiency [forty-seven].
The pigeon presented had a peri-bulbar tumour and surgery to remove it a few weeks before succumbing to avian malaria.
Furthermore, on histopathology, there was evidence of a thyroidal neoplasm.
These factors may have contributed to the demise of the bird.
Our PCR results showed a coinfection with Leucocytozoon spp.
AEMOtwo in the adrenal gland.
This lineage was first reported in feral pigeons in southern Italy and in a cinereous vulture(Aegypius monachus) in Spain [ten].
However, the pathogenicity of this lineage is not described.
Analysis of impression smears and organ histology did not show any gametocytes or exoerythrocytic stages (meronts or megalomeronts) of Leucocytozoon.
The fact that only one organ was PCR-positive may be suggestive of a previous or new infection with low parasitaemia that may only be detected by PCR.
However, these scenarios could not be confirmed in this study.
Coinfections of Plasmodium and Leucocytozoon are common in naturally infected hosts [ten, forty-nine].
Coinfections may affect the host fitness and the pathogenicity of the parasite species or lineage [thirty-seven, forty-nine].
This scenario may be true in the current case as a virulent P. malariae.
Relictum GRWeleven infection may have masked an effect of the Leucocytozoon infection.
This poses a challenge as it requires personnel training to visualize and identify the parasite stages.
Other authors have used chromogenic in-situ hybridization (CISH) with Plasmodium-specific probes to stain parasites in the tissues [forty-five, fifty].
Anti-P. falciparum HSPseventy has been used for the detection of P. falciparum and Plasmodium berghei mosquito, hepatocyte and erythrocytic stages [fifty-one].
Evidently mature parasites (gametocytes and schizonts) showed an increased staining in IFA and IHC compared to immature ones (trophozoites).
This may be difficult to interpret on IHC as cut sections of tissues are used and this may modify the appearance of the parasite staining.
Berghei parasite stages [fifty-one, fifty-two].

Relictum and may be used to aid the diagnosis of avian malaria.
Relictum infections in pigeons are less frequently reported, sporadic occurrences may be fatal.
The bird most likely died from severe anaemia due to high blood parasitaemia from an acute P. falciparum.
Relictum GRWeleven infection with moderate pneumonia and hepatitis.
Infected erythrocytes in tissues and blood vessels of various organs were seen microscopically, but no exoerythrocytic meronts were seen.
The study presents for the first time use of an anti-P. falciparum HSPseventy antibody for use in immunostaining methods to detect P. vivax.
Relictum parasites in the blood.
Necropsy analysis further revealed a Leucocytozoon coinfection and thyroid carcinoma in the bird.
These conditions may have exacerbated the Plasmodium infection, resulting in the bird succumbing to infection.
Further analysis of pigeons complemented previous studies and suggest that avian Plasmodium infections are uncommon in pigeons in Switzerland.

Malaria Journal A global mathematical model of climatic suitability for Plasmodium falciparum malaria Owen Brownone, Jennifer A.
Mathematical models relating climatic conditions to malaria transmission can be used to develop spatial maps of climatic suitability for malaria.
These maps underpin efforts to quantify the distribution and burden of malaria in humans, enabling improved monitoring and control.
Previous work has developed mathematical models and global maps for the suitability of temperature for malaria transmission.
In this paper, existing temperature-based models are extended to include two other important bioclimatic factors
The addition of humidity and then rainfall improves the comparison (ρ = zero point sixty-two)

This burden is predominantly focussed in sub-Saharan Africa, where ninety percent of the continent’s population resides in P. falciparum malaria endemic areas [one].
High-resolution maps of malaria prevalence and incidence are therefore critical for measuring progress in tackling malaria.
Spatial variation in malaria transmission intensity is driven by myriad factors, including
These models to predict how changes in local climate and environment may alter malaria risk.
Attempts to generate global maps of climatic suitability for P. falciparum malaria have typically focussed on a single aspect
[sixteen] extended this work by applying the same model to high temporal- and spatial-resolution observed temperature data derived from satellite imagery.
Furthermore, this shortcoming necessitates the inclusion of variables that characterize moisture conditions in subsequent malaria burden models.
This enables climatic suitability mapping for malaria globally, and with greater biological realism than previous studies.
The modelling framework employs mathematical relationships between the environmental metrics and the Anopheles mosquito life-cycle.

In terms of the discrete-time model, in each cohort, the sporozoite development value Yi was also tracked (Step three, Fig. twenty-one).
Here Yi represents the number of degree days passed.
Once Yi reaches a critical threshold value of ddev, the sporozoite is considered to be fully developed.
During this non-biting period, no members of the population can become infected, so development of the sporozoite cannot occur.
It is assumed that members of the cohort become infected immediately after this non-biting period ends.
After the initial non-biting period, it was assumed that one percent of the remaining cohort would become infected [thirty-six, thirty-seven].
It is acknowledged that this is a simplification of reality and possible extensions are discussed later in the discussion.

The study aimed to implement a valid Simulated Malaria Online Tool (SMOT) for assessment HCP performance in CMSM and POR in a malaria-free area.
Multiple logistic regression analysis was carried out to estimate adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for the risk of HCPs failures.
Results The overall failure proportion was two hundred thirty-seven (eighty-three percent), and the majority of failures were in recognition (a).
There was no significant difference between the SMOT and SP based on all failure criteria (P > zero point four).
The private clinic (ninety-three percent) and the public specialized clinic (seventy percent) had the highest and lowest failure proportions.
After passing the recognition stage (a), the overall failure proportions decreased to forty-seven point zero  percent.

Conclusion Findings confirmed the implementation of SMOT tool in settings where malaria transmission is low or interrupted.
The tool is able to identify sub-groups of providers needing strengthening, and contributes to the prevention of malaria re-establishment.

For sampling, the roster of all HCPs in East Azerbaijan province (N = four thousand, nine hundred fifty-three) was acquired through Tabriz University of Medical Sciences.
HCPs were selected using stratified random sampling.
The questionnaire link was sent to them through an online method (email, social network, or SMS).
In the case of non-response, a provider of the same type and stratum was randomly chosen from the entire population of that stratum.
The study response rate was eighty-eight.
Measurement (implementation of SMOT) HCPs’ practice in CMSM was assessed using SMOT, which has been validated by Azizi et al.
[one] with the same categories of HCPs as in the current study and in the same area.
The sensitivity and agreement of SMOT in comparison with the simulated patient methodology considered the gold standard were ninety-eight.
SMOT was made available on an online platform with link (https
Ir/s/sSfqXFQ), and sent to HCPs through email and/or virtual networks.
Although respondents were aware of their assessment, they did not realize it was related to malaria [one].
The design allows for every question to be answered based on the previous responses.
If the respondent asks about their travel history as part of their response to the previous question(s), the travel history details will be triggered.
Finally, SMOT considered HCPs into two groups of failure and pass.
Providers were classified in the failure group if they failed in at least one of the four criteria (a), (b), (c) and (d).
Flowchart and details of SMOT performance and structure is presented in Appendix one.
Details of the tool’s performance and psychometric properties have been reported previously [one].
Statistical analysis The SPSS software (version twenty-one point zero).
Chicago, IL, USA was used for data analysis.
The Chi-square (χtwo) test was used to examine categorical variables.
Independent t-test was conducted for quantitative variables when normal distribution and homogeneity of variance were met [eleven, twelve].
For modelling, all independent variables were initially evaluated through simple logistic regression.
Subsequently, variables with a p-value below zero.
two underwent further analysis via multiple logistic regression employing the Enter method.
The Hosmer and Lemeshow statistic was utilized to assess data congruence and the model’s goodness of fit [twelve, thirteen].

Therefore, one reason for the high failure rates of HCPs is the lack of consideration for the health system’s performance beyond just HCPs.
Among specialists, the failure rate was the lowest, while personal and private clinics had the highest failure rate.
These results underscored the effective performance of public (governmental) health facilities in the national malaria control program.
Consistent with the current study findings, Selemani et al.
In Tanzania[sixteen] found that HCPs with work experience of more than three years were more successful in case management.
Strengthen and limitation Evaluation of healthcare providers’ actual performance requires real cases in the field.
However, in areas where malaria transmission has been interrupted, real cases are scarce.
To address this issue, the study utilized SMOT to simulate real-life scenarios.
This may slightly elevate the likelihood of failure compared to real-life situations.
Healthcare providers’ adherence to appropriate malaria case management, especially in detecting suspected malaria cases, needs improvement.
Meanwhile, implementing and evaluating healthcare providers’ practices using SMOT is crucial in preventing malaria re-establishment.

However, there is still need for targeted interventions in the study area to promote LLIN use among caregivers of under-fives.
In most households, children and women were prioritized to sleep under the LLIN.
Women and children, compared to youths and men, have been shown to be regular users of LLINs in literature [two, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-three].
A major reason for this may be because women and children are often perceived to have higher risk of malaria infection [twenty-two].
Furthermore, the physical integrity and cleanliness of the nets were maintained in most of the households.
The physical durability of nets has been strongly linked with duration of use with median survival rates of three point seven years observed in past studies [thirteen].
seven years observed in past studies [thirteen].
A higher proportion of younger children (< three years) slept under the LLIN.
Findings from other published works in sub-Saharan African countries support this [twenty, twenty-four].
Another possible reason is the common practice of younger children sleeping with their mothers under LLINs until they are fully weaned [eight].
This practice in the study area could contribute to the higher reported LLIN use among children under three years compared to older children.

Parents with higher levels of education were more likely to ensure their children slept under LLINs.
This has been observed in previous studies conducted in Nigeria [nine], Ethiopia [twenty-six], and Ghana [twenty-seven].
This may be attributed to the increased knowledge and understanding of malaria and its prevention methods among educated individuals [nine, twenty-eight, twenty-nine].
This further attests to the fact that educational attainment of parents or guardians is a major social determinant of child health.
This finding brings into focus the important role of proper LLIN maintenance in malaria prevention.
Proper cleaning of LLINs and replacing them at due time may have an enhanced effect on malaria control.
Households with more than six members and four or more nets were more likely to have LLINs with holes.
The results may inform targeted interventions for improving malaria control in such contexts.
In addition, future studies will be required to deepen the understanding of contextual factors that may hinder the effective use of LLINs.

Parasitology tests Microscopic examination of Hemacolor rapid-stained impression smears revealed an asynchronous infection of haemoparasites (Fig. two).
Round and irregularly shaped trophozoites were seen and mature trophozoites displaced the host erythrocyte nucleus.
Erythrocytic meronts containing up to eighteen merozoites, with characteristic clumped-up haemozoin pigment were seen.
Round gametocytes with scattered haemozoin pigment were present in the blood film and most displaced the host erythrocyte nucleus (Fig. three).
The parasitaemia was determined to be approximately eighteen percent.
Immunofluorescence assay using anti-P. falciparum HSPseventy antibody revealed red immunopositive reactions corresponding to different parasite stages (Fig. four).
The antibody staining was diffusely distributed in the parasite cytoplasm.
The adrenal gland had a coinfection with Leucocytozoon spp.

Follow‑up The other pigeons of the owner were reported to be in good health.
The owner was advised to isolate wild/feral birds and test them before mixing with his pets.
Adoption of wild birds is not advised unless approved by veterinary authorities.
Wild birds may harbour diseases that are transmitted to pets and/or to humans.
It is also unadvisable to move birds between geographical borders, as this may spread diseases between regions.
In January twenty twenty-four, another dead pigeon was submitted to the NRGK by the same owner.
Upon necropsy, the bird was emaciated.
The gizzard contained two broken paperclips.

Discussion This case describes avian malaria infection in a feral-pet pigeon, as confirmed by an extensive diagnostic work-up.
The major finding in this study is P.
This is the first time this lineage has been reported in a pigeon (Columbiformes).
Information on the pathogenicity of this lineage in natural infections is lacking.
Experimental infections of GRWeleven in canaries have reported mild infection with low parasitaemia during the acute phase, in contrast to P. falciparum.
Relictum SGSone which is known to cause high parasitaemia in canaries [thirty-seven].
In the case presented here, the pigeon infected with P. knowlesi.
Relictum GRWeleven had high parasitaemia and evidently all erythrocytic stages of the parasite were present.
When the rate of erythropoiesis cannot compensate for the erythrocyte loss through destruction, anaemia is inevitable [thirty-eight].
Hill CM [thirty-nine] reported severe anaemia due to reduced number of erythrocytes as a proximate cause of death in pigeons infected with P. knowlesi.

Malaria Journal (twenty twenty-four) twenty-three
These changes are often seen in avian malaria infections [forty].
Infection with Plasmodium triggers inflammatory infiltrates of leukocytes.
Monocytes, lymphocytes or heterophils), and these were noted in various organs [forty-one, forty-two].
This has been reported in previous studies with avian, human, and rodent malaria infections [twenty-six, forty-three].
This factor may have contributed to the bird succumbing to infection.
Exoerythrocytic meronts (phanerozoites) were not seen in the examined organs.
These parasitic forms are mostly known to originate from natural or sporozoite inoculated infections [twenty-eight].
Phanerozoites may be differentiated from the phagocytosed erythrocytic meronts that we observed in this study by their lack of haemozoin pigment.
Relictum infections, exoerythrocytic meronts are limited once the blood infection is established [twenty-eight, forty-four].
Recent publications have reported the absence of phanerozoites in P. ovale.
Relictum infections in wild and experimental birds and some authors suggest that some strains of P. knowlesi.
Relictum may not develop phanerozoites altogether [twenty, thirty-seven, forty-five].
In canaries, phanerozoites were observed in endothelial cells of brain capillaries [thirty-eight].
However, in a more recent study, these parasite stages were not detected in experimentally infected canaries [forty-five].
Farmer JN and Moore AK [forty-six] reported death in ten out of thirty-eight P. knowlesi.
Relictum experimentally infected pigeons during the course of infection.
In four of the ten dead birds, phanerozoites were observed mostly in the brain and some in the liver and spleen.
In another study on P. malariae.
Relictum-infected puffins, phanerozoites have been observed in two out of three infected birds, in the liver, spleen, kidney, lung and heart [twenty-six].
These studies suggest that the development of exoerythrocytic parasite forms may be dependent on the parasite strain and/or the avian host infected.
The physiological state of the host during infection plays a major role in determining infection outcome.
For example, hosts in poor health may be predisposed to infectious diseases due to immunodeficiency [forty-seven].
The pigeon presented had a peri-bulbar tumour and surgery to remove it a few weeks before succumbing to avian malaria.
Furthermore, on histopathology, there was evidence of a thyroidal neoplasm.
These factors may have contributed to the demise of the bird.
Our PCR results showed a coinfection with Leucocytozoon spp.
AEMOtwo in the adrenal gland.
This lineage was first reported in feral pigeons in southern Italy and in a cinereous vulture(Aegypius monachus) in Spain [ten].
However, the pathogenicity of this lineage is not described.
Analysis of impression smears and organ histology did not show any gametocytes or exoerythrocytic stages (meronts or megalomeronts) of Leucocytozoon.
The fact that only one organ was PCR-positive may be suggestive of a previous or new infection with low parasitaemia that may only be detected by PCR.
However, these scenarios could not be confirmed in this study.
Coinfections of Plasmodium and Leucocytozoon are common in naturally infected hosts [ten, forty-nine].
Coinfections may affect the host fitness and the pathogenicity of the parasite species or lineage [thirty-seven, forty-nine].
This scenario may be true in the current case as a virulent P. malariae.
Relictum GRWeleven infection may have masked an effect of the Leucocytozoon infection.
This poses a challenge as it requires personnel training to visualize and identify the parasite stages.
Other authors have used chromogenic in-situ hybridization (CISH) with Plasmodium-specific probes to stain parasites in the tissues [forty-five, fifty].
Anti-P. falciparum HSPseventy has been used for the detection of P. falciparum and Plasmodium berghei mosquito, hepatocyte and erythrocytic stages [fifty-one].
Evidently mature parasites (gametocytes and schizonts) showed an increased staining in IFA and IHC compared to immature ones (trophozoites).
This may be difficult to interpret on IHC as cut sections of tissues are used and this may modify the appearance of the parasite staining.
Berghei parasite stages [fifty-one, fifty-two].

Relictum and may be used to aid the diagnosis of avian malaria.
Relictum infections in pigeons are less frequently reported, sporadic occurrences may be fatal.
The bird most likely died from severe anaemia due to high blood parasitaemia from an acute P. falciparum.
Relictum GRWeleven infection with moderate pneumonia and hepatitis.
Infected erythrocytes in tissues and blood vessels of various organs were seen microscopically, but no exoerythrocytic meronts were seen.
The study presents for the first time use of an anti-P. falciparum HSPseventy antibody for use in immunostaining methods to detect P. vivax.
Relictum parasites in the blood.
Necropsy analysis further revealed a Leucocytozoon coinfection and thyroid carcinoma in the bird.
These conditions may have exacerbated the Plasmodium infection, resulting in the bird succumbing to infection.
Further analysis of pigeons complemented previous studies and suggest that avian Plasmodium infections are uncommon in pigeons in Switzerland.

The study is not without limitations.

Conclusion The study assessed the impact of routine use of RTS,S malaria vaccine on uncomplicated malaria among children aged twelve–fifty-nine months.
The vaccine reduced episodes of uncomplicated malaria by thirty-three percent.
Although the malaria incidence averted decreased marginally over time, the impact on uncomplicated malaria remained significant.

Hence, this study aimed to assess the determinants of urban malaria, focusing on the role of urbanization and the distribution of An.
Stephensi in Eastern Ethiopia.
Methods A matched case control study was conducted among febrile urban residents of Dire Dawa (malaria positive as cases and negative as a control).
Then, the data were exported to STATA for analysis.
Conditional logistic regression was done to identify determinants, and principal component Analysis (PCA) was done for some independent variables.
Results This study enrolled one hundred thirty-two cases and two hundred sixty-four controls from urban setting only.
Of the one hundred thirty-two cases, ninety cases were posi‑ tive for Plasmodium falciparum, thirty-four were positive for Plasmodium vivax and eight had mixed infections.
All cases and con‑ trols were similar with regard to their respective age and sex.

Com Full list of author information is available at the end of the articleMerga et al.
Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax are the most prevalent, and P. falciparum is the most virulent species [one–four].
The co-existence of these two species makes malaria control more complicated [five–seven].
Most of these cases were coming from countries in the World Health Organization (WHO) African Region [eight].
The WHO and UN (United Nations) Habitat indicated that by twenty fifty nearly seven out of ten people globally will live in cities and urban settings.
Unplanned growth of urbanization and the spread of the invasive malaria vector Anopheles stephensi make malaria control in urban areas difficult.
The spread of this vector into Africa further complicates the already complex malaria situation.
This vector appears to swiftly acclimate to its surroundings and thrives in manmade water containers in urban settings.
For urban malaria control strategies to be successful, it must be directed at the urban areas where infections are occurring.
If infections are contracted in cities, similar actions must be targeted differently.
Because of this, effective urban malaria control depends on accurate clinical and epidemiologic data [eighteen].
Therefore, this study identified urbanassociated socioenvironmental determinants of urban malaria in Eastern Ethiopia.
Dire Dawa is one of the two city administrations in the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia with about four hundred sixty-five thousand populations.
It is located between ninety twenty-eight.
one″ N latitude and between forty-one and fifty.
There are two public hospitalsMerga et al.

Febrile patients who visited the health facilities, either tested positive or negative, from rural areas were excluded from the case control study.
Cases were defined as clients from urban areas only who had malaria illness by meeting three criteria

Knowledge To assess the participants’ knowledge on malaria, its control and prevention, twelve knowledge related questions were used.
An overall knowledge score was calculated by adding all scores for each respondent for all knowledge related questions.
Attitude Attitude was assessed using thirteen attitude related Likert scale questions.
An overall attitude score was calculated by using principal component analysis and finally dichotomized as poor and good.
Data collection tool and procedure Data were collected by ODK software with the tool developed from different relevant and related literatures.
The questionnaire was translated to both Afan Oromo and Amharic languages and back translated to English to check for consistency.
Both thick and thin blood smears were prepared on a clean, labeled microscopic slide for each selected study participant.
Finally, the slides were stained with ten percent Giemsa for ten min, air dried, and examined microscopically by an experienced laboratory technologist.
The slides were considered negative if no parasite was seen after examining one hundred high power fields.
To ensure the quality of data, pretest was done among five percent of the sample size at Laga Hare Health center in Dire Dawa city.
Data were downloaded from the Open Data Kit (ODK) server and appropriate cleaning was done before further analyses using Stata version sixteen (Stata Corp.College Station, TX, USA).

Recently licensed life-saving vaccines have experienced slow introduction and gradual uptake in the developing world.
Policy challenges at the national level contribute to the delay in making new vaccines accessible to people in poor countries.
Epidemiologic and economic analyses can help facilitate their decision-making.
The majority of people who die of malaria are children less than five years of age.
Malariarelated mortality has not decreased in the past decade, and by some estimates has actually increased.
Increasingly, international attention is focused on developing vaccines that can prevent malaria.
New funding is allowing scientists from the public and private sectors to reinvigorate their efforts to accelerate malaria vaccine development.
There are multiple policy challenges in making a vaccine accessible to the people who need it most.
When a new vaccine becomes available, decision-makers will have questions about it.
Previous investigators have offered frameworks for such decision-making.
Aylward and others proposed a framework for evaluating vaccines for use in the Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI).
one Mansoor and others proposed a framework for assessing new vaccines.
Figure one shows the likely factors in national decision-making about malaria vaccine introduction.
Policymakers in malariaendemic countries facing such a decision will want to compare the potential impact of a malaria vaccine.
Its ability to reduce morbidity and mortality rates, with the impact of other malaria control and treatment interventions.
They will also want to compare it to the potential impact of other health and development interventions.
The public health impact of a malaria vaccine will depend in part on the characteristics of the vaccine.
Without a licensed malaria vaccine, any discussion about a vaccine profile is purely hypothetical.
And the decision to introduce the actual vaccine will pose policy challenges that will require further analysis.

MALARIA CONTROL AT THE DISTRICT LEVEL IN AFRICA
The data were collected from nineteen ninety-six to two thousand three in the Muheza district northeastern Tanzania.
All six members of the district health management team were also interviewed.
Additional data came from dispensary and hospital records, and published literature.
The results show an unchanged malaria disease burden.
The average number of clinical malaria episodes per child less than five years of age remained between three and three point five episodes per year.
three point five episodes per year in the district since the nineteen sixtys.
Furthermore, between nineteen ninety and two thousand three, little training on malaria was provided to health staff.
The operational responsibilities of malaria control were transferred to the district level under the guidance of ministries of health.
For example, the role of primary health workers within the district was made more complicated as tasks were added.
It was clear that for the strategy to succeed, re-training and re-deployment of primary health workers at all levels was crucial.
Primary health care through the District Health Services (DHS) has an important role in the control of malaria.
three This report presents the results of a study analyzing the effectiveness of the DHS in the Muheza District of Tanzania regarding malaria control.
MATERIALS AND METHODS Study area.
The Muheza District is one of the seven districts in Tanga region in northeastern Tanzania.
The district has thirty-five wards with a population of two hundred seventy-nine thousand, four hundred twenty-three.
four An average ward has approximately eight thousand people.
The population growth rate is one point eight percent compared with the national average of two point four.
one point eight percent compared with the national average of two point four.

Mortality in children less than five years old in the Muheza District is two hundred eight/ten thousand eight which twenty-six percent higher than the national average of one hundred sixty-five/one thousand.
nine The district has thirty-two dispensaries, three health centers, and one district hospital.
Primary health care through the District Health Services (DHS).
It occurs throughout the district with the exception of few pockets in the eastern Usambara Mountains.
eight Plasmodium falciparum is the main causative agent, accounting for more than ninety percent of all the infections.
Determinants of the epidemiology and clinical impact of malaria for the Muheza District are ecology, transmission, and immunity.
ten Throughout the district and similar to other malariaendemic areas, immunity to malaria varies by age.
eleven At birth, children have acquired immunity from their mothers.
twelve They are not only protected against clinical disease, but can also clear infection spontaneously following infective bites.
This immunity is lost rapidly within three months and children develop their own immunity slowly over time.

Regulation of drug use
The results on sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine are shown in Figure four.
The proportion of treatment failures is shown in two separate studies to be more than eighty percent between nineteen ninety-five and nineteen ninety-seven.
Resistance to chloroquine in Muheza was first documented by the reported resistance rate of five percent reported by Clyde.
The same level of resistance was reported in another study in nineteen sixty-six.
In nineteen seventy Lelijveld and Mzoo reported a resistance rate of ten percent.
In nineteen eighty-five, the median in vivo resistance to chloroquine in school children documented by Kilimali and Mkufya was twenty percent.thirty-one.
Mutabingwa and others later reported a resistance rate of eighty percent in infants, fifty-eight percent in children one–five years old, and fifty percent in children six–ten years old.
Similar results were reported by Rønn in nineteen ninety-seven, who showed a resistance rate of seventy percent in children less than five years of age.
Overall, the review shows a high level of treatment failures for cases treated with chloroquine in the period from nineteen ninety-five to two thousand three.

MALARIA IN PRIMARY SCHOOL CHILDREN AND INFANTS IN KINSHASA, DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF THE CONGO
The most complete information on malaria prevalence in Kinshasa was first acquired in nineteen eighty-one−nineteen eighty-three.
Blood smears were obtained from twenty-five thousand, one hundred thirty-five children (ages five−fifteen years) from two hundred forty-five schools in sixteen of twenty-four zones.
The mean Plasmodium falciparum parasite rate was seventeen percent; the parasite rate was similar for both sexes and was higher (P < zero point one) in older students.
The primary anopheline mosquito control measure.
The parasite rate varied from four percent (urban zone) to forty-six percent (peri-urban zone).
An infant survey confirmed malaria transmission.
A mean parasite rate of thirty-four percent was found among school children five−nine years old.
The parasite rate varied from fourteen percent (central urban zone) to sixty-five percent (peri urban zone).
Plasmodium falciparum was not the only species found, but accounted for more than ninety-seven percent of the infections.
Malaria incidence may have increased in Kinshasa during the last two decades due to difficulties in provision of control and prevention measures.
Malaria is primarily a rural disease, but can be a serious problem in urban areas.
five Since these cities are usually major international centers, the disease can be exported to nonmalarious areas.
BACKGROUND Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is a prime example of an urban population explosion.
Its population has grown from three hundred eighty thousand in nineteen sixty to two million, seven hundred thousand in nineteen eighty-two and to more than five million, two hundred ninety-three thousand in two thousand three, an increase of almost fourteen times in forty years.
The city is administratively divided into twenty-four administrative zones or communes that cover some nine thousand, nine hundred sixty-five kmtwo.
According to the national health policy, twenty-four health zones (HZs) roughly cover the twenty-four administrative zones.
One zone, Maluku, has an area of seven thousand, nine hundred forty-eight kmtwo or eighty percent of the area.
Kinshasa is on the southern bank of the Congo River and part of its peri-urban area is bordered by a large marsh with an area of approximately sixty-five kmtwo.
In nineteen seventy-seven, Ward found Anopheles gambiae in most types of water, including polluted water, in Kinshasa.
eight Historically, Kinshasa has been a malarious area.
These zones were chosen for historic, geographic, and logistic reasons.
Ndjili, Masina, and Kimbanseke are peri-urban and new settlements, while Limete is an old central urban zone.
Operational activities began in the zone of Ndjili in nineteen seventy-nine and in the zones of Limete, Masina, and Kimbanseke in nineteen eighty.
The primary anopheline mosquito control measure was intradomiciliary spraying with DDT.
To obtain this information, school surveys were conducted during an eighteen-month period, beginning in late nineteen eighty-one.
In addition to the school surveys, a fifteen-month study was conducted in the Limete zone where newborns from two hospitals were registered monthly.
Efforts were made to collect monthly blood smears from all infants registered during that period.
In late nineteen eightys, with the interruption of the bilateral cooperation, USAID left Kinshasa and malaria activities stopped.
In nineteen ninety-eight, a new malaria control program, the Program NaAm.
To obtain this information, school surveys were conducted.
In nineteen ninety-nine, the country endorsed the global “Roll Back Malaria” (RBM) strategy.
One area thus explored was the prevalence of infections in school children.
These recent findings are reported in this paper.
Early surveys (nineteen eighty-one–nineteen eighty-three).
A list of the primary schools in each of the twenty-four zones was obtained from the Department of Education or from zonal offices.
Each school was located on a city map for field personnel use and for plotting malaria prevalence by zone.
Authorities at each school were also informed that at a second visit one hundred thick and thin blood smears would be taken from twenty-five students in four classes.
Both students and classes were selected by a table of random numbers.
Only students from the zone being sampled were included, but this residency requirement could be as short as one day.
Any child reporting a fever at the time the smear was taken was treated with a single dose (ten mg base/kg of body weight) of amodiaquine.
Plasmodium falciparum was sensitive to the four-aminoquinoline drugs in Kinshasa at the time the surveys were performed.
The blood smears were stained with Giemsa, and one hundred thick smear fields were examined on each smear.
The thin smear was used for species identification.
To assess whether transmission was occurring in Kinshasa, infants born in two hospitals in Limete zone were registered.
This was done monthly for fifteen months.
Visits to the infants each month were made to monitor their malaria status during the past month.
Informed consent was obtained following the procedures of the Program de Lutte Antipaludique.
In turn, school administrators were responsible for obtaining parental consent.
Verbal consent was also obtained from the guardians of each infant enrolled in the newborn infant follow-up survey.
Recent surveys (two thousand).
In each school, only students five−nine years old were targeted.
A one hundred-blood smears sample was collected from students that were present.
Blood smears were stained with Giemsa and read by an experienced microscopist.
In September two thousand, this survey was repeated in five of these ten schools from five communes (Barumbu, Kalamu, Kimbanseke [Kikimi HZ], Ngaba, and Ngaliema).
During this second stage, only students living in the HZ area were included in the sample to allow for comparison between different sites.
Students who were positive were given sulfadoxinepyrimethamine (SP) in a single dose (one point twenty-five mg/kg of body weight of pyrimethamine).
one point twenty-five mg/kg of body weight of pyrimethamine plus twenty-five mg/kg of body weight of sulfadoxine.
This was done because a recent in vivo drug study confirmed its efficacy, as well as a high level of chloroquine resistance.
fifteen Sulfadozine-pyrimethamine was the second-line antimalarial drug when the surveys were done.
Although this survey was considered a routine procedure of minor risk, it was reviewed and approved by a Ministry of Health technical committee board.
The parents of the children were also contacted for informed consent.
Survey staff held meetings with parents, teaching staff, and parent/school committees.
The survey was conducted once consent was obtained.
Early surveys (nineteen eighty-one−nineteen eighty-three).

Zone parasite rates varied from four percent in Lingwala (downtown Kinshasa) to forty-six percent in Mont Ngafula (a peri-urban area).
Within zones, the individual school parasite rates varied from zero percent to ten percent in Lingwala, and from fifteen percent to eighty-four percent in Mont Ngafula.
Of the twenty-one thousand, eight hundred ninety-four smears examined in thirteen of the zones, four thousand seventy-eight (nineteen percent) were positive (Table three).
There was no significant difference in parasite rates by sex in any age group, but the parasite prevalence rates increased significantly (P < zero point one).

INTRODUCTION
Over the last fifteen years, it has become apparent that malaria causes significant morbidity in terms of neurologic and cognitive impairment.
This represents a hidden and poorly defined public health consequence of malaria, particularly in Africa.

Limitations of the studies.
In the review of the studies, a number of limitations were identified.
They can be categorized as follows.
Differences in definition.
There are considerable differences in the definition of the parameters used in these studies.
Thus, some studies use the strict definition of CM proposed by the WHO,seven while others use a more functional definition.

eleven twelve These differences are further confounded by differences in the pathogenesis of the strictly defined clinical complications.

Audiometry for hearing.
The definition of cognitive impairment varied considerably from clinical judgment to standardized psychological tests.
Some studies did not identify the proportion of children with impairment, but compared the scores between cases and controls.
Furthermore, some studies were randomized control trials of interventions that may have affected the outcome.
fourteen–sixteen This makes the generalization of the results difficult to compare with other areas in Africa.
Differences in assessment.
Clinicians and assessors vary in their ability to assess children.
The ability of clinicians to detect neurologic deficits varies according to experience and the circumstances in which the examination is conducted.
Most studies do not report the interobserver variation or experience of the clinicians in assessment techniques.
In the studies shown in Table three, mild sequelae were often detected when the child was examined in an outpatient setting.

Confounding factors.

Entomologic inoculation rates, malaria prevalence, and vectors in urban Africa.
We generated a comprehensive database on malaria transmission in urban and peri-urban African settings, as expressed by EIR and malaria prevalence.
The EIR is defined as the number of infective bites per person per time unit.
Two previous papers have compiled EIRs for urban and rural settings in sub-Saharan Africa.
We only included data from urban areas that have a population of ten thousand inhabitants or more.
In many instances, we estimated EIRs from age-specific malaria prevalence data using the mathematical model of the Garki project.
twenty-two This method has been recently described by Hagmann and others.
It is defined by a set of difference equations that specify the change in each of these proportions from one time point to the next.
Within this model, the EIR is approximated by the product C*yone, where yone is the proportion of the human population that is infective.
twenty-five Asymptotic ninety-five percent confidence estimates were obtained by numerical estimation of the Fisher information.
This procedure gives minimum estimates of the EIR because the model was developed on the assumption that none of the infections are treated.
We also implemented the simple version of the model that assumes a constant vectorial capacity throughout the year.
This also leads to lower estimates of the EIR than would be obtained if seasonal transmission was assumed.
We also reviewed the literature with regard to the main malaria vectors and summarize their habitat preferences, particularly for the larval stages.

Objectives
Describe the pathophysiology of malaria infection.
Summarize the pharmacologic treatment strategies for malaria infection.
Outline the importance of collaboration amongst an interprofessional team to improve outcomes for patients receiving malaria treatment.

Two billion people risk contracting malaria annually, including those in ninety endemic countries and one hundred twenty-five million travelers.
seven million people die in a year.
The Plasmodium parasite has a multistage lifecycle, which leads to characteristic cyclical fevers.
Preferred antimalarial therapeutic and chemoprophylactic regimens get dictated by species, geography, susceptibility, and patient demographics.
Latent or reactivating infections may be reported years following exposure.

P. falciparum is present in Western and sub-Saharan Africa and displays the highest morbidity and mortality of the Plasmodia species.
P. vivax is present in South Asia, the Western Pacific, and Central America.
P. ovale and P. malariae are present in Sub-Saharan Africa.
P. knowlesi is present in Southeast Asia.
As many as five hundred million malaria cases occur annually.
Ninety percent of fatalities occur in Africa.
Go to
The female Anopheles mosquito ingests gametes during a blood meal, which form sporozoites that replicate in the gut.
During subsequent bloodmeals, saliva containing sporozoites gets released into a human host's bloodstream.
Within sixty minutes, sporozoites reach the liver, invade hepatocytes, and then rapidly divide, forming merozoites.
In an active infection, organisms reenter the bloodstream and invade erythrocytes.
Free heme is released into the peripheral blood, which stimulates endothelial activation.
Untreated malaria lasts two to twenty-four months.
Pathogenesis stems from toxin-induced IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha secretion.
The innate immune response is dominated by monocyte and macrophage phagocytosis within the splenic red pulp.
Adaptive immunity develops by IFN-gamma and TNF-alpha-induced class switching of CDfour-positive lymphocytes.
TNF also suppresses hematopoiesis, which contributes to anemia.
The liver and spleen enlarge, causing massive splenomegaly.
Low arginine, low nitric oxide, and elevated arginase activity have been observed in severe malaria in peripheral blood.
Low nitric may lead to subsequent pulmonary hypertension and myocardial wall stress in children.
Therefore, peripheral arginine or inhaled nitric oxide are possible treatment options.
Parasitemia dictates symptom onset and severity
two percent parasitemia in naïve patients and zero.
two percent parasitemia in previously exposed patients.
Severe infection usually exhibits parasitemia of five percent.
They are more likely to develop hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and severe anemia without major organ dysfunction than adults.
In semi-immune pregnant women, only a few infections result in fever or other symptoms.
Anemia is typically moderate with P. vivax and P. malariae due to preferential invasion of reticulocytes and older erythrocytes, respectively.
The coagulation panel may reveal coagulopathy concerning bleeding risk in patients with severe thrombocytopenia or liver dysfunction.
Urinalysis may show proteinuria indicative of nephrotic syndrome.
The extent of parasitemia is estimated by the number of organisms per high-powered field.
The malarial pigment in monocytes and neutrophils may also manifest on the blood smear, particularly in patients with cerebral malaria.
Other diagnostic modalities include rapid diagnostic testing (RDT), microhematocrit centrifugation, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
Sensitivities approach one hundred percent, though microscopy is still a recommendation at the time of presentation and twelve and twenty-four hours.
PCR is useful in low-level parasitemia detection and speciation.
Higher initial parasitemia and poor downtrend are associated with fluid imbalance, renal dysfunction, and respiratory distress syndrome.
Unstable patients, particularly those with cerebral malaria or significant respiratory sequelae, require intensive care.
Treatment involves combination therapy targeting both the hepatic and erythrocytic forms.
The chief antimalarials are chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, primaquine, artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), and atovaquone-proguanil.
Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are synthetic forms of quinine.
They disrupt the erythrocytic stage by interfering with parasitic hemoglobin metabolism and increasing intracellular pH.
They generally require two days of treatment, allowing for better tolerance and shorter admissions.
However, chloroquine may enhance gametogenesis, contributing to resistance, which is a concern, particularly in South Asia.
Artemisinins are active against all parasite lifecycle stages.
Atovaquone-proguanil is active against the erythrocytic and extraerythrocytic forms.

P. falciparum and P. ovale infections last two to three weeks and may relapse six to eighteen months later, usually from a new primary infection.
P. vivax infection lasts three to eight weeks and may relapse months to up to five years later.
P. malariae infection lasts three to twenty-four weeks and may relapse up to twenty years later.
Appropriate, complete treatment usually results in a full resolution of symptoms.
While the general mortality of treated severe malaria is between ten to twenty percent, the mortality in pregnant women reaches approximately fifty percent.
Go to
Cerebral malaria accounts for eighty percent of fatal malaria cases, most often occurring with P. falciparum infection.
It most commonly affects children under age five, with a case fatality rate of eighteen percent.
Increased brain volume is the major contributor to mortality in cerebral malaria.
Nephrotic syndrome is common in P. malariae and P. knowlesi, possible in P. vivax, and rare in P. falciparum and P. ovale infections.
Algid malaria is an adrenal insufficiency due to parasitic congestion and subsequent necrosis of the adrenal glands.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome, circulatory collapse, disseminated intravascular coagulation, pulmonary edema, coma, and death.
Malaria infection during pregnancy may result in low birth weight or fetal demise.
Malaria prevention centers around vector control and chemoprophylaxis while exposed to mosquito-ridden environments.
The three main prophylactic agents for Plasmodium falciparum are atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, and mefloquine.
Doxycycline is taken once daily during and one month after travel; it suppresses the blood stage.
Mefloquine is taken once weekly during and one month after travel; it suppresses the blood stage.
It has the benefit of safety in the second and third trimester of pregnancy; however, it has a far higher risk of neuropsychiatric side effects.
The US military primarily utilizes doxycycline if susceptibilities are equal.
Any clinician treating malaria will initiate treatment as outlined above.
This collaborative interprofessional approach can optimize outcomes for malaria patients.

However, the few existing studies show that severe malaria in children imposes a significant economic burden on the providers and households.
More studies are needed, particularly in high‑burden high‑impact countries, to inform resource allocation decisions.
The recent World Malaria Report estimated that in 2022, malaria caused 249 million cases and 608,000 deaths globally [1].
About 95% of these deaths occurred in Africa, and about 80% of them were in children younger than five years.
Four of these countries.
Nigeria, DR Congo, Niger, and Tanzania, were responsible for just over half of all malaria deaths [1].
In 2022, the total expenditure on malaria control and elimination globally was estimated at USD 4.1 billion, of which 80% went to Africa [1].
$1 billion, of which 80% went to Africa [1].

Search strategy and selection criteria Four databases including PubMed, Embase, Cinahl and Web of Science were systematically searched.
The search had no date restrictions, and the last search was conducted on January 04, 2024.
All studies, which involved children below 12 years old were included.
Other inclusion criteria were that studies were conducted in malaria-endemic countries in Africa, they focused on the management of severe malaria (i.
Malaria requiring hospitalization) and reported primary cost data.
Studies that exclusively relied on secondary data and studies on travelers from non-endemic countries were excluded.
An additional file shows all the search terms used for each database (see Additional file 1).
Figure 1 is the PRISMA flow diagram.
All identified articles and reports were screened by two researchers, GM and ATM independently and assessed for eligibility.
Any disagreement was resolved by consensus, or by a third reviewer.
Provider costs were those borne by the health facilities and household costs were borne by the patients’ caregivers.
The societal costing perspective included both the provider and household costs.
Quality assessment Quality assessment was conducted independently by ATM and GM.
An 8-item checklist was developed from Drummond et al.
Bottom-up, top-down, or a combination; (iii) the sources of resource utilization data.
Quality was assessed by scoring each item with a value of ‘1’ if fully completed.
5’ if not fully completed, ‘0’ if not completed and ‘NA’ if not applicable.
The quality scores were categorized as ‘low’ if ≤ 33%, ‘moderate’ if the score was between 34 and 66% and ‘high’ if > 66%.

Household payments that exceeded 10% of this income were assumed to constitute Catastrophic Health Expenditure (CHE)[11].

Conclusion Evidence about the cost of managing severe malaria in children in Africa is relatively scarce.
Despite the stated limitations, the existing studies show that the disease imposes a significant economic burden on the health system and households.

The annual rainfall was extracted from the Climate Hazards group Infrared.
Precipitation with Stations (CHIRPS) dataset.
Starting from twenty fourteen to twenty twenty-two.
Rainfall averages were extracted per state (three).
The estimated cases for each state.
Were calculated as a function of the modeled incidence estimates and the projected.
Population for that state.
As described in the World malaria report twenty twenty-two (four).
Population estimates used in this report are based on projections by state of the two thousand six.
Nigeria national census.
The World malaria report twenty twenty-two that is based on UN national population projections.
Affecting the overall estimates of cases.
Estimated cases averted over the period two thousand nine–twenty twenty-one were computed by comparing.
Estimates for each year since two thousand nine with the malaria case incidence rates from two thousand nine.
Adjusting for population growth.
The year two thousand nine was selected as the baseline (or.
Counterfactual in the absence of interventions) considering that this was the year.
When first mass insecticide-treated nets (ITN) campaigns were implemented.
Data on distribution of ITNs and SMC were provided by the NMEP.
Malaria prevalence.
Treatment seeking.
Diagnosis and ITN coverage indicators were extracted from the.
Household survey reports.
Health facility level monthly IPTp data were extracted.
The number of first and second doses of IPTp and the total number.
Of first antenatal care visits were aggregated to calculate the national and state.
Level coverage of IPTpone and IPTptwo per year.
Coverage was calculated by dividing.
The number of IPTpone or IPTptwo doses by the total number of first antenatal care visits.
Reports that had missing data for one or more of the data elements were excluded.
From the analysis.
Data were checked for consistencies and outliers.
When appropriate.
To improve data quality.

Donor financing for malaria has declined between twenty ten and twenty thirteen.
And this trend is projected to continue for the foreseeable future.
These reductions in external financing are even greater for the sub.
Set of malaria eliminating countries despite demonstrated evidence on the returns on investment from elimination.
Income countries and therefore a lesser priority for donors.
While domestic spending on malaria appears to be growing.
It varies substantially in speed and magnitude across countries.
As the disease becomes less “visible.
government funds for malaria are often diverted to other health priorities that are perceived to be greater health threats.
Risking a reversal of the recent gains made in malaria elimination.
These changes come at a critical time when commitment to elimination will be crucial to paving the way to global malaria eradication.
A clear understanding of spending patterns and trends in donor and domestic financing is needed to uncover critical investment gaps and opportunities.
We teamed up with the Institute for Health Metrics & Evaluation to look at the trends in Development Assistance for Health (malaria health programme) and Government Health Expenditure (Rate of occurence) for malaria eliminating countries from nineteen ninety to twenty thirteen with projections to twenty seventeen.
This is the first study that tracks malaria health programme and Rate of occurence for malaria eliminating countries in a systematic way.

The study assessed the impact of the RTS,S malaria vaccine on uncomplicated malaria episodes among children aged twelve–fifty-nine months.
The trend of vaccine uptake reflects the pathway of the introduction process in the region and the country at large.

The study is not without limitations.
Further, only data from facilities reporting in DHIMS-two were used for the study.
Data from private health facilities, community pharmacies and alternative practitioners were unavailable.
Furthermore, the impact of the vaccine on severe malaria was not assessed due to inadequate data.
Lastly, attribution rates for IRS, and LSM for the study areas, respectively, could not be estimated due to incomplete data.
The application of attribution rates from other studies could impact reliability of the results.
Conclusion The study assessed the impact of routine use of RTS,S malaria vaccine on uncomplicated malaria among children aged twelve–fifty-nine months.
The vaccine reduced episodes of uncomplicated malaria by thirty-three percent.
Although the malaria incidence averted decreased marginally over time, the impact on uncomplicated malaria remained significant.

Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax are the most prevalent, and P. falciparum is the most virulent species [one–four].

The WHO and UN (United Nations) Habitat indicated that by twenty fifty nearly seven out of ten people globally will live in cities and urban settings.
Unplanned growth of urbanization and the spread of the invasive malaria vector Anopheles stephensi make malaria control in urban areas difficult.
The spread of this vector into Africa further complicates the already complex malaria situation.
This vector appears to swiftly acclimate to its surroundings and thrives in manmade water containers in urban settings.
Moreover, the vector has also exhibited resistance to several classes of insecticides.
Urbanization has significant epidemiological, entomological, parasitological, and behavioural implications on malaria risks.
The global patterns of disease and mortality, including malaria, will change due to a shift in the human population from rural to urban areas.
Besides, the epidemiology of urban malaria since the spread of a new mosquito vector species, An.
Stephensi, in sub-Saharan Africa, including Ethiopia, is not well studied [twelve].
For urban malaria control strategies to be successful, it must be directed at the urban areas where infections are occurring.
If infections are contracted in cities, similar actions must be targeted differently.
Because of this, effective urban malaria control depends on accurate clinical and epidemiologic data [eighteen].
Therefore, this study identified urbanassociated socioenvironmental determinants of urban malaria in Eastern Ethiopia.
