This protozoan disease is caused by Plasmodium parasites
This protozoan disease is caused by Plasmodium parasites and  transmitted through the bite of female Anopheles mos quitoes.
A number of species of Plasmodium can infect  humans, with Plasmodium falciparum responsible for  over ninety-nine percent of malaria-related deaths [two].
Malaria is sensi tive to climate factors, including temperature, rainfall,  and humidity, which influence mosquito breeding and  parasite development.
In  the same year, global malaria-related deaths were esti mated at six hundred eight thousand, with a mortality rate of fourteen.
Three deaths per  one hundred thousand people at risk.
Over fifty percent of total deaths occurred in just  four countries: Nigeria (thirty-one percent), the Democratic Repub lic of the Congo (twelve percent), Niger (six percent), and Tanzania (four percent).
From two thousand to twenty twenty-two, malaria incidence in the  Fig.
Malaria eradication will only be achieved when all  human-infecting Plasmodium parasites are eradicated  globally [eight].
Malaria Journal Page three of nine diphtheria, tetanus, and rabies [nine].
The eradication of  smallpox demonstrated the power of vaccination in  combating infectious diseases globally.
However, early  efforts to create a malaria vaccine were met with signifi cant challenges.
T he first promising studies for a malaria vaccine  emerged in nineteen sixty-seven, when mice were immunized using live,  radiation-attenuated sporozoites.
These early results demonstrated  the potential for a vaccine against malaria.
These advancements have paved the way for  ongoing research efforts to develop an effective malaria  vaccine for widespread use in humans [eleven].
T he RTS,S vaccine is one of the earliest malaria vac cine candidates that eventually achieved success [twelve].
In the nineteen eightys, scientists at the Walter Reed Army Insti tute of Research (WRAIR) in the U.
Their approach aimed to stimulate  the immune system by using the circumsporozoite pro tein (CSP), a surface protein of the sporozoite.
Although  previous attempts to target CSP had failed, GSK scientist  Joe Cohen proposed a new strategy.
He used a hepatitis  B virus surface protein (HBsAg) as a scaffold to present  CSP, creating a virus-like particle to enhance the immune  response.
A major breakthrough came with the development  of a human challenge model by WRAIR, enabling the  team to safely infect human volunteers with P.
Falcipa rum and test various vaccine candidates.
This involved  infecting Anopheles mosquitoes with malaria para sites and allowing vaccinated volunteers to be bitten,  monitoring them for infection.
Volunteers who became  infected were promptly treated with anti-malarial drugs.
Large scale human trials followed, initially in adults, then in  adolescents, children, and infants in malaria-endemic  regions of sub-Saharan Africa.
In twenty fifteen,  the European Medicines Agency (EMA) granted a posi tive opinion for the use of  Mosquirix in children aged  six weeks to seventeen months.
Pilot programmes were initiated  in Malawi, Ghana, and Kenya by twenty nineteen to evaluate the  vaccine’s real-world impact [fifteen].
Like RTS,S, Rtwenty-one targets the circum sporozoite protein (CSP) found on the surface of P. Falciparum
P.Falciparum sporozoites, but with important enhancements.
This modification enhances the density  of CSP on the virus-like particle, improving the vaccine’s  immunogenicity.
This  approach avoids the dependency on excess hepatitis B  surface antigen (HBsAg) required by RTS,S, streamlin ing the production process [nineteen].
Following a WHO recommendation, several Afri can countries incorporated malaria vaccination into their  national immunization programmes.
Cameroon became  the first country to implement routine malaria vac cination on January twenty-two, twenty twenty-four [twenty-three].
AMVIRA seeks to  enhance technical assistance to Member States, facilitat ing the effective introduction and deployment of malaria  vaccines.
Malaria vaccination in Africa has demonstrated signifi cant impact.
The success of the  MVIP and insights gained from the pilot programme  played a crucial role in guiding the development of the  Rtwenty-one malaria vaccine.
This achievement reflects the growing potential of  vaccination programmes in curbing malaria’s burden  across endemic regions [twenty-seven].
Smallpox, once  claiming over three hundred million lives with a mortality rate of  thirty percent, was eradicated in nineteen seventy-seven through a WHO-led vacci nation efforts [twenty-six].
Immunization efforts have since saved  one hundred fifty-four million lives over fifty years, reducing global infant  mortality by forty percent and contributing ten.
Two billion healthy years to populations worldwide.
The  COVID-nineteen pandemic further underscored vaccination’s  value, spurring the largest immunization campaign in  history [thirty-one, thirty-two].
T his momentum has been steadily building, with more  than half of the world’s countries now malaria-free.
Annual spending on malaria increased  from approximately one dollar.
Five billion in two thousand to four dollars.
Three billion in  twenty sixteen, resulting in a thirty-six percent decline in malaria incidence and  a sixty percent reduction in mortality.
In contrast, the  WHO has been cautious about committing to a specific  timeline.
The WHO projections indi cate that, using existing tools, Africa may still face eleven mil lion malaria cases by twenty fifty [thirty-six].
In this context, malaria  vaccination emerges as a potentially transformative  intervention.
When effectively implemented, vaccines  can significantly reduce transmission rates, complement ing other preventive and treatment measures.
Malaria vaccination not only offers significant health  benefits but also demonstrates cost-effectiveness.
For sub-Saharan Africa, with an average GDP  Sibomana et al.
Malaria Journal               Page five of nine per capita of USsixteen thirty-six dollars.
Eight, according to the World Bank  Group [thirty-nine], a malaria vaccine would be cost-effective  if its cost per DALY averted was under USfour thousand, nine hundred ten dollars.
A  study by Schmit et al.
Further analysis reinforces the cost-effectiveness of  malaria vaccines, even with a higher vaccine cost.
A  model by Kelly et al.
The median cost  per DALY averted was estimated to range from USfour hundred eighty dollars  to USsix hundred eighty-two dollars.
In moderate to high transmission settings,  the cost per DALY averted dropped to between USone hundred seventy-five dollars  and USone hundred eighty-seven dollars [forty-one].
Investments in malaria control are not only health enhancing but also yield significant economic returns.
Between twenty eleven and twenty fourteen, malaria control cost only  USfive dollars–eight per case averted, generating millions in sav ings.
Countries with malaria see zero.
An expenditure impact  study found that for every USone dollar invested in malaria  control in Africa, there is an increase of USsix dollars.
Seventy-five in per  capita GDP, further demonstrating the economic value of  investing in malaria vaccination and elimination efforts  [forty-three, forty-five].
GAVI, the Vaccine  Alliance, has committed USone hundred fifty-five dollars.
Seven million to support  the RTS,S vaccine rollout in Ghana, Kenya, and Malawi  through pilot programs [forty-six].
Despite these efforts, the Global  Technical Strategy for Malaria twenty sixteen–twenty thirty estimates that  funding requirements will increase from USsix dollars.
Eight bil lion in twenty twenty to USten dollars.
Therefore, while malaria  vaccination has proven cost-effective, continued invest ment is needed to meet the growing demand for these  interventions.
The primary issue  lies in the efficacy of available vaccines, which do not  provide complete protection against malaria.
Additional  challenges include vaccine shipment and storage difficul ties, as well as infrastructure and logistical constraints.
Inadequate funding and resource allocation for malaria  vaccination programs further hinder progress.
Furthermore,  a lack of understanding regarding the malaria vaccine  among healthcare workers exacerbates the problem.
The genetic diversity of Plasmodium parasites poses  a significant challenge to malaria control.
This genetic  variability limits the long-term efficacy of existing vac cines and complicates their application in different geo graphical areas.
Many areas, particu larly in sub-Saharan Africa, have underdeveloped health care infrastructure, making vaccines distribution difficult.
Poor road networks hinder access to remote areas, and  Sibomana et al.
Malaria Journal Page six of nine healthcare facilities often lack the cold chain storage nec essary to maintain vaccine efficacy.
In addition, health care systems are frequently overwhelmed, and ensuring  follow-up with patients may be inconsistent [fifty-two].
A further complication lies in integrating malaria vac cines into existing immunization programmes.
Vaccines  like RTS,S require four doses, making coordination with  existing childhood immunization schedules complex.
Vaccine hesitancy is another significant challenge in  implementing routine malaria vaccination.
In many Afri can communities, misinformation, cultural beliefs, and  mistrust of healthcare systems drive skepticism toward  vaccines [fifty-six, fifty-seven].
T hese limitations hinder efforts to protect vulnerable  populations, particularly in areas where the disease bur den is highest.
Ensuring a stable supply of vaccines is  essential for successful malaria control and eventual  eradication.
To achieve this, sustained financial sup port from governments, global health organizations,  and private-sector donors is critical.
Overcoming the barriers to effective malaria vac cination in Africa requires a coordinated, multi-level  approach.
Scientifically, continued innovation in vaccine  development is critical to improving both efficacy and  coverage.
Emerging technologies, innovations, and interventions  are pivotal in supplementing these efforts.
Artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced technolo gies hold great potential in the fight to eradicate malaria  [sixty-two].
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) can facili tate in real-time surveillance, mapping high-risk areas,  and monitoring outbreaks.
In addition, devices such as SolarMal and ThermaCell  repellents have also been used to reduce mosquito popu lations [sixty-three].
Malaria Journal Page seven of nine approach has long been controversial.
ATSBs combine sugar-based  baits with toxicants to attract and kill mosquitoes, prov ing effective across different ecological contexts.
Trials  in Zambia demonstrated ATSBs’ ability to target Anoph eles species, the primary malaria vectors [sixty-seven].
Nonetheless, ATSBs  align with sustainable pest management and offer a viable  alternative to traditional insecticides.
Recent studies have underscored the potential  of mAbs, particularly LnineLS, which has demonstrated sig nificant efficacy in clinical trials [seventy-three].
LnineLS specifically  targets the sporozoite stage of P. falciparum, blocking  the parasite’s attachment to liver cells and promoting its  destruction.
By binding to a key protein on the sporozo ite, LnineLS interrupts the malaria life cycle [seventy-four].
In a phase  two trial, LnineLS showed sixty-six–seventy-seven percent efficacy in preventing P.
Falciparum infection in children [seventy-three].
Further research is essential to improve the  efficacy of existing vaccines and develop more effective  alternatives.
Comprehensive,  multi-faceted approaches will be necessary to fully  address this complex public health challenge.

Edu Abstract  Nigeria bears the highest global burden of malaria, accounting for twenty-five percent of cases  and nineteen percent of deaths worldwide.
Development partners provide substantial support for  malaria prevention and treatment in Nigeria.
We conducted an interview-administered household  survey in urban, semi-urban and rural regions in Enugu State in twenty twenty.
We collected  data on the use of malaria services and out-of-pocket (OOP) payments.
Socioeco nomic status (SES) was estimated using household assets ownership.
A concen tration index was used to assess equity in spending on malaria across socioeconomic  quintiles.
We estimated the gross and net benefit incidences for malaria services by  deducting the OOP payment from the gross benefits.
Most respondents were women,  married, and had attained secondary education.
Nine percent of surveyed households  owned bed net.
Six percent of households used malaria drugs in the past months.
All users paid OOP for malaria drugs, sprays and lab services and over one-third of  households incurred OOP costs for bed nets.
The total OOP expenditure for malaria  in the past month was zero dollars.
The gross benefit incidence for malaria  services was eighteen thirty-six dollars.
The net benefit and donor benefit were sixteen seventy-nine dollars.
Both gross and net benefit for malaria services favored less-poor house holds.

Introduction Malaria is a significant public health challenge in ninety-seven countries and territories [one].
Malaria places a considerable strain on Nigeria’s health system and households.
Over forty percent  of outpatient consultations, thirty percent of hospitalizations, and eleven percent of maternal mortalities in Nige ria were attributed to malaria in twenty eighteen.
The financial burden of medical and  related costs presents a significant barrier to seeking proper care for malaria [ten].
Malaria services are predominantly funded by development partners.
In twenty twenty-one, the Enugu state  government’s expenditure on long-last insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) was a mere zero.
Seven percent of  the total health budget, amounting to Nten million, six hundred sixty thousand million [thirteen].
In contrast, development  partners contributed over ninety-nine percent of the funding for malaria.
From twenty fourteen to twenty seventeen, donor financ ing for malaria in Nigeria totaled one dollar.
Fifteen billion with Global Fund being the largest contributor  (one hundred seventy-nine dollars.
Enugu state has allocated varying budgets to support different malaria control programs in  recent years.
In twenty twenty-one, only Nten million was allocated for  the procurement of LLINs.
As Nigeria transitions away  from donor assistance, concerns arise about sustaining the progress made in malaria con trol.
Understand the benefit inci dence of donor-funded malaria programs.
This paper aims to assess which households have  benefited the most from these programs.
Materials and methods Study sites The study was conducted in three Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Enugu state, southeast  Nigeria.
Enugu State, with its capital city, Enugu, is made up of seventeen LGAs, five of which  are urban, while the remaining are rural.
The state has an estimated population of four.
Five million  people [twenty-three].
Additionally, there are about seven hundred private health facilities, consisting of private and non profit, private for profit, and faith-based facilities.
The  selected areas included the state capital (urban and semi-urban) and Nkanu West (rural).
In  twenty nineteen, the malaria prevalence was estimated at twenty-seven.
Six percent in Enugu state [eighteen].
We conducted government, donors and  malaria services documents review to collect the unit cost of different malaria services.
Six percent in southeast Nigeria [twenty-four].
A minimum sample of five hundred sixteen households for the survey  was estimated.
Primary Healthcare (PHC) numbering system was used to determine house holds for the survey.
Then other households were picked after every alternative household until the total number of  respondents were collected across the selected LGAs.
Data collection Household survey was conducted between February ten-twenty-eight, twenty twenty using interviewer-  administered pre-tested structured questionnaires.
Primary care giver or in his/her absence,  the male head of each selected household was interviewed.
Respondent in each household  provided information on malaria prevention and treatment for the entire household mem bers.
The questionnaire was administered by trained field workers to the sample of randomly  selected household members.
The household questionnaire has three sections: demographics, socioeconomic status and  individual household health expenditure.
The one-month recall  period was used to reduce the incidence of recall bias for a longer period.
We collected the medical and non-medical costs associated with malaria services in the  study areas.
Medical expenditures are costs incurred in the prevention or treatment of injury  or disease.
Non-medical costs on the other hand include additional  costs in accessing healthcare such as transport and meals.
Data analysis We used STATA and SPSS software packages to analyze the data.
The distributions of the key  variables were analysed across socioeconomic status (SES) and rural-urban location.
We analysed the use of different types of malaria services and then estimated the total  healthcare costs.
The total health service use per month include outpatient, diagnosis and  treatment.
Costs were calculated in official local currency (Naira, N), then converted to US Dol lar at the rate of Nthree hundred sixty.
Zero to one (one) US$ in twenty twenty.
Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric test, which  reports a Chitwo statistic was used to compare differences in means of continuous variables.
Concentration index was used to measure the level of equity in the distribution of bene fits.
Asset holding of the respondents were compared with the DHS data twenty eighteen.
This was possi ble because questions on asset ownership were similar to the DHS data.
The approach was  to describe the SES of respondents in study sites with reference to the national population.
Principal component analysis was used to compute weights for the ownership of identified  list of assets in the twenty eighteen DHS data.
The weight scored were used to determine the scores for  each SES.
Written informed consent form was obtained and signed by all respon dents.
Primary care giver or in his/her absence, the male head of each selected household was  interviewed.
Data collectors were duly trained on handling confidential information from the  respondents.

Discussion This study analysed the use, financial burden and benefit incidence of malaria services in  Enugu, Nigeria.
Among the survey respondents, over half of households owned a bed net, and  about one-third used malaria drugs in the past months.
All users have paid OOP for malaria  drugs, sprays and lab services while over a third paid OOP for bed nets.
Both the gross and net  benefits for malaria bed nets and other services were pro-rich among the survey respondents.
About one-third of the surveyed households used malaria drugs in the past month.
Bed nets and  sprays are preventive measures, while over half of the surveyed households owned bed nets,  only one.
Despite this, the overall use of malaria preventive approaches remains  relatively low in Enugu, Nigeria.
Rural and poorer households also need greater  attention.

The study also revealed that wealthier households benefited from donor funded bed nets than the poorer households.
The financial burden of malaria services may contribute to the underuse of malaria  diagnostic services in Nigeria.
According to the survey, all or most households paid OOP for  malaria drugs, lab services, RDTs and sprays.
It is also important to note that this study found that rural residents spent more on total  OOP (zero dollars.
Ninety-eight) than their urban counterparts (zero dollars.
These factors enable  them to demand care through more cost-effective options compared to rural residents.
The total gross benefit for malaria services among the surveyed households was eighteen thirty-six dollars.
Seven,  with malaria drugs contributing the most, followed by bed nets.
Our study revealed inadequate use of malaria services, a heavy financial burden, and a pro rich distribution of benefits.
Reports from Enugu State Ministry of Health from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-three indicate specific govern ment budgets allocated for malaria treatment and control.
However, such benefits, including funding for indoor  residual spray or “free” malaria drugs, were not observed in this study.
All households that  used malaria drugs paid OOP, likely at a subsidized cost.
Additionally, only one.
Seven percent of surveyed  households used the spray.
This evidence suggests a need for increased promotion and fund ing for malaria services in Enugu State and Nigeria as a whole.
This study has several limitations.
As a result, the burden of malaria care may have been underestimated.
Second,  although a one-month recall period is commonly used in major household surveys, we  acknowledge that it may still be affected by recall bias.
Third, the use of wealth index as a  ten / thirteen PLOS Global Public Health https://doi.who.org
Further research is  needed to better understand households’ financial coping strategies for seeking care and the  role of existing malaria programs.
Lastly, IPTp, a core components of PMI funding, was not  included in the analysis due to a lack of data.
Conclusion and policy implications This study examined the use, financial burden and the benefit incidence of malaria services  in Enugu state.
The study found that financial spending and use of malaria services are not  equitable.
There is a clear need for improved access to affordable malaria prevention and  treatment services in the state.

Ajayione  Abstract  Background Effective malaria control in under-five children depends on caregivers seeking timely medical care.
However, despite available healthcare services, many caregivers do not utilize health facilities, undermining malaria  control efforts.
Methods A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted in Ondo State, Southwestern Nigeria.
The study areas  were Ifedore, Ondo East, and Idanre Local Government Areas (LGAs) randomly selected from the eighteen LGAs  in Ondo state.
A multistage sampling technique was used to select participants and data was collected using a struc tured questionnaire.
Results The study included three hundred one caregivers of under-five children, predominantly aged twenty-six–forty-five years (sixty-nine.
Eight percent compared to females (forty-nine.
One percent residing in rural areas.
Four percent of caregivers identified  infected mosquito bites as the cause of malaria, and ninety-eight.
Three percent recognized fever as a main symptom, only fifty-one.
Two percent dem onstrated good overall knowledge of malaria and symptoms in under-five children.
Zero percent of caregivers  suspected malaria in their under-five children within twelve months prior to the study, however, only nine.
Three percent visited a health  facility for treatment of their under-five children.
Four percent purchased drugs from patent medicine vendors  and pharmacies, while twenty-five.
Two percent used herbs for home management.
Bivariate analysis showed significant associations  between health facility visits and being a female caregiver (p  equals to zero.
Nine), urban residence (p  equals to zero.
Two), residing within five km  of a facility (p  equals to zero.
Twenty-one), and good malaria knowledge (p  equals to zero.
Multivariate logistic regression indicated that female  caregivers (aOR  equals to three.
Fifty-four), urban residents (aOR  equals to four.
Forty-eight), residing within five km  of a health facility (aOR  equals to three.
Seven), and those with good malaria knowledge (aOR  equals to four.
Seventy-seven) were significant predictors of visiting a health facility for malaria care for under-five children with suspected  malaria by caregivers.

It remains a major  global public health concern, with sub-Saharan Africa  recording the highest burden [one–three].
Among the most  vulnerable populations, children under-five experience  a disproportionate share of malaria-related morbidity  and mortality [one–three].
Nigeria has the highest malaria burden globally, with  the disease being a leading cause of childhood mortal ity [five].
Eight percent  of global malaria deaths, with children under-five being  the most affected [six].
Care-seeking behaviour among caregivers plays a  crucial role in the timely management of childhood ill nesses, including malaria [seven–ten].
More  importantly, malaria treatment outcomes in children  under-five are closely linked to caregivers’ health-seek ing behaviour [thirteen].
Previous research on malaria care-seeking behaviour  among caregivers in Nigeria highlights key trends and  gaps [fourteen–sixteen].
However, delayed healthcare-seeking in health  facilities remains a major concern in Nigeria [fourteen–sixteen].
Regional disparities in healthcare access and cultural  influences further shape malaria care-seeking behaviour  in Nigeria [fourteen–sixteen].
Methods Study area Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa, with an  estimated population of over two hundred twenty million [seventeen, eighteen].
It has  six geographical zones with varying ecologies, climates,  and population characteristics.
Ondo state, where the study was conducted, is located  in Southwestern Nigeria (Fig.
Additionally,  hunting and livestock rearing, particularly goats, sheep,  and fish, are prevalent occupations.
The state’s economic  landscape also encompasses trading, civil service, and  various government employment opportunities [twenty-two].
Study design A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted using a  questionnaire survey method.

Ninety-six); P  equals to proportion of caregivers of under f ive children with good malaria health seeking behav iour; d  equals to acceptable difference (if five percent, d  equals to zero.
T he prevalence estimate was obtained from a previous  study where eighteen.
Six percent of caregivers utilized health facilities  for malaria treatment of their under-five children in Imo  state, Nigeria [nine].
Sampling method A multistage sampling technique was employed in this  study.
In stage three, three wards were selected from the list of wards  in each selected LGA using a simple random technique  (balloting).
A total of eighteen settlements were ran domly selected from the list of settlements generated  from each LGA.
In stage five, households were sampled from each selected  settlement using a spatial systematic random sampling  with a random start technique.
The middle of each settle ment was identified, and then a pen was tossed.
Sampling  started from the house in the direction of the tip of the  pen.
For settlements with less than twenty houses, one house  was skipped, while two houses were skipped for settle ments with more than twenty houses.
Sampling continued  until the required sampling size expected for the settle ment was reached [twenty-one, twenty-three].
Finally, in stage six, eligible caregivers of under-five chil dren in each selected household who met the inclusion  criteria were interviewed.
A household was defined as a  group of people living together daily in the same house  and sharing meals from the same pot [twenty-one].
Field practical training  was conducted on the third day of the training.
Thereaf ter research assistants proceeded to the field for data col lection which spanned for ten days.
Data were collected  using paper-based questionnaires.
The supervision of  data collection was done by the principal investigator.
Data analysis T he data obtained were entered into a secured file struc ture on IBM Statistical Package for Social Sciences  version twenty-five.
Zero and analysed using frequency counts, per centages, cross tabulations, and logistic regression analy sis with p  lesser than zero.
Five level of significance.
For knowledge score  of malaria and symptoms in under-five children among  caregivers, respondents were scored using a fifteen-item  question.
A point was assigned to the correct response  to each question.
The total score of each participant  was divided by the total expected score (fifteen points) and  multiplied by one hundred to derive the percentage score.
A modi f ied Bloom’s cut-off was adapted to classify knowledge  levels, using a sixty percent threshold as the distinction between  good and poor knowledge.
Bloom’s taxonomy is widely  used in educational and health research to categorize  learning and comprehension levels (Bloom).
T he final model was interpreted using adjusted odds ratio  (AOR) and corresponding ninety-five percent CI.
Also, Informed consent was  obtained from the respondents.
Before data collection,  respondents were approached individually by trained  research assistants and given a detailed explanation of  the study.
The explanation was provided in a language  (English, Yoruba, or Pidgin) that the respondents were  comfortable with to enhance comprehension.
They were  reassured that their decision would not affect their access  to healthcare services or other benefits of the study.
If literate, they were asked to read and sign  the form.
Signed or thumbprinted forms were securely stored as  Page five of twelve Akinrinade et al.

T his study has some limitations.
Firstly, the care seeking behaviour reported in this study was based on  suspected malaria by caregivers thus some cases may  not have been malaria.
However, trained interviewers were engaged  for this study as well as a well-structured questionnaire  was used for the data collection.
Additionally, probing  questions were asked to ensure correct responses were  provided by the respondents during the interviews.
Fur thermore, the cross-sectional design of this study limits  the study to descriptive and associative interpretations.
This approach could  discourage the use of unauthorized malaria treatment  among caregivers of under-five children.

Abstract Background: Malaria is a significant source of mortality and morbidity, particularly among children  under the age of five.
Therefore,  this study investigates the sociodemographic factors associated with malaria among under-five children  in Nigeria.
Methodology: This study used secondary cross-sectional data collected from the twenty eighteen Nigeria  Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS).
The sample for this study was ten thousand, three hundred fifty-two children.
Analysis was done using bivariate analysis and binomial logistic regression at a zero.
Five  significance level and ninety-five percent confidence interval.
Results: Children's age was statistically significant with malaria (Xtwo  equals to one hundred sixty-six).
Malaria had a  statistically significant relationship with mother’s level of education (Xtwo  equals to seven hundred sixty-two).
The  relationship between malaria and wealth index was statistically significant (Xtwo  equals to ten twenty).
The result shows that children living in rural areas were more prone to have malaria infection than  children living in urban areas (OR  equals to one.
Therefore,  broad-based programmes and interventions should be increased to tackle malaria incidence and  prevalence.

Variables  For this study, the malaria RDT results of children aged six-fifty-nine months were used as the response variable.
Those who tested positive are coded as one, and those who tested negative are coded as zero.
The independent  variables were used as already numerically coded in the dataset, while the children's age was recoded into  five categories.
These factors were  selected based on the findings presented by Nyarko & Cobblah [nine] and Paul & Msengwa [twelve].
Then, eight hundred forty-five children with missing variables were excluded.
Therefore, ten thousand, three hundred fifty-two under-five children comprised the final sample for this study.
Data Analysis  Data were analysed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version twenty-fivein two steps.
Data analysis and interpretation were  conducted at a zero.
Five level of significance and ninety-five percent confidence interval (CI).

Globally, there are approximately two hundred forty-nine million reported cases of malaria, leading  to six hundred eight thousand deaths (WHO twenty twenty-three).
Nigeria, in particular,  contributes significantly, up to twenty-seven percent of all malaria cases worldwide (WHO twenty twenty-three).
Effective malaria case management is a crucial and widely used method for  malaria control.
Chloroquine (CQ), introduced in the mid-nineteen fortys, was once the cornerstone of  malaria treatment due to its effectiveness, safety, and affordability.
Twenty twenty-one), and prompted a global review of malaria treatment  policies.
They function by disrupting the digestion of hemoglobin during the blood stages  of the malaria parasite’s life cycle (Combrinck et al.
These mutations alter the parasite’s susceptibility to CQ and other antimalarials  (Roux et al.
Pfcrt and pfmdrone are vital transporters within Plasmodium,  serving dual roles as mediators of drug resistance and as drug targets.
Initially, the mutation in  pfcrt and pfmdrone was recognized for their involvement in conferring chloroquine  resistance (Fidock et al.
Nineteen ninety), but are now known to influence  parasite’s susceptibility to numerous contemporary antimalarial drugs (Cheruiyot  et al.
The emergence of parasite resistance to artemisinin derivatives and partner drugs  in ACT poses a significant threat to malaria control.
However, such resistance has  not yet been reported in Nigeria’s Pfkelchthirteen propeller domain (Igbasi et al.
Twenty nineteen;  Abubakar Zubair et al.
ACTs remain effective in treating malaria across the  majority of regions in Nigeria (FMOH-NMEP, twenty fifteen) (WHO twenty twentya; Oyebola et al.
Furthermore, resistance is rising in the Greater Mekong Sub-region and parts  of Africa, including Rwanda and Uganda (Ashley et al.
Twenty twenty-one;  Uwimana et al.
Molecular surveillance of drug resistance markers is crucial for monitoring  and maintaining treatment efficacy (Uwimana et al.

Lagos is located at six.
Seven thousand, five hundred degree East in the South-Western region of Nigeria, with an altitude of forty m (one hundred thirty-one feet).
It shares  its borders with Ogun State to the north and east, the Republic of Benin to the west,  and the Atlantic Ocean to the south (Fig.
The city has a coastline of approxi mately one hundred eighty km, characterized by lagoons, creeks, and swamps.
These water bodies  are separated from the open sea by a sandy land strip, varying in width from two to  sixteen km.
Lagos experiences a tropical climate, with most months marked by signifi cant rainfall and a short dry season.
The area is holoendemic for malaria, with a  mean temperature of twenty-six.
Seven degree celsius (ranging from twenty-nine to thirty-five degree celsius), an annual mean relative  humidity is eighty-four.

The region accounts for over ninety percent of global malaria  cases and deaths [one].
Effective prevention and timely treatment are essential  to malaria control strategies to reduce disease incidence  and improve health outcomes.
Higher educational attainment can enhance health  literacy and empower individuals to adopt preventive  behaviours.
Exploring  the nuanced relationship between education and malaria  prevention behaviours in rural populations remains a  priority.
Mass media campaigns have been widely used to raise  awareness and encourage treatment-seeking for malaria  [fourteen].
This study also seeks to  address some unanswered questions in malaria preven tion efforts.
For household-level analyses on malaria prevention  (ITN ownership and use), the final sample consisted of  Alao et al.

This composite measure is based on asset own ership, housing characteristics, and service access.
This grouping created more precise comparisons  between households with similar economic backgrounds.
For the exclusion criteria, households with missing ITN  ownership or usage data were not included in the anal ysis.
This was important to ensure the data was reliable  and that incomplete information would not affect the  results.
The dependent variables included two key indicators  related to malaria prevention.
The dependent variables in this component consisted  of malaria prevention awareness and preventive meth ods.
Respondents answer ing “Yes” to either indicator were classified as aware.
The dependent variable in this section was the type  of healthcare service accessed for malaria treatment.
Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS  Statistics Version twenty-seven.
Chi-square tests were  applied to assess statistical significance.
Row percentages  were reported to describe the prevalence of outcomes  within each category.
Survey weights were applied to  account for the complex stratified sampling design used  in the MIS datasets.
To estimate independent associations, multivariable  analyses were conducted.
A multinomial logistic  regression model was employed to analyse media expo sure and healthcare access, treating the type of healthcare  Alao et al.

Media exposure was  entered as a binary predictor representing frequent ver sus infrequent exposure.
Model fit was evaluated using Nagelkerke R² for binary  logistic regression models and pseudo R² statistics for  the multinomial model.
The Hosmer-Lemeshow good ness-of-fit test was applied to binary logistic regression  models.

Categori cal data were displayed primarily as grouped bar charts  to compare subcategories within income and education  groups.
Percentage values were annotated on bars for  clarity, and clear labels and titles were included to ensure  interpretability.

This finding aligns with  other studies reporting widespread ITN access following  intensified national malaria control efforts [fifteen, sixteen].
Several plausible expla nations exist.
However, the inverse relationship between education  and reported net use contrasts with the positive associa tion between education and awareness.
Women with no  education were more likely to sleep under a mosquito net  the night before the survey than those with higher educa tion levels.
This discrepancy may reflect complex socio cultural and contextual factors.
Seasonal fluctuations, reported discomfort,  or alternative preventive measures may also contribute.
This lack of association persisted after adjusting for potential con founders in multinomial logistic regression models.

T he study’s findings have several practical implications.
Tailored messaging that addresses perceptions,  convenience, and alternative protection strategies may  enhance ITN adherence.
Second, increasing malaria  prevention awareness through education is critical, but  insufficient alone to ensure net use.
T here are several reasons why media exposure was not  significantly associated with treatment-seeking behaviour  in this study.
Even when  media campaigns are widespread, the content may not  resonate with local values, beliefs, or language, limit ing its effectiveness.
Another reason could be the struc tural barriers to healthcare access.
In many rural areas,  these barriers can be just as significant as awareness, if  not more so.
Lastly, passive exposure to media without  active engagement or trust in the messaging may also  contribute to the lack of significant impact.
This underscores the importance  of increasing media exposure and ensuring that messages  are engaging, credible, and trusted by the target audience.
T his study has limitations.
The wealth index, while a standard proxy for  socioeconomic status, may not capture all dimensions  of economic variation.
Furthermore, media exposure  was broadly defined and did not assess content, message  quality, or comprehension.
Additionally, several unmeasured confounders may  influence the observed relationships.
For example, differ ences in local malaria transmission intensity could affect  both ITN use and treatment-seeking behaviour.
In addition, the media exposure analysis, with a sample  size of n  equals to eight hundred ninety-three, is smaller than the other analyses in this  study.
As such, its findings should be interpreted with  caution, and the conclusions drawn from this smaller  sample may not be as generalizable.
Further research  with larger sample sizes is needed to confirm these find ings.
Future research should employ longitudinal designs to  capture temporal changes in malaria prevention behav iours more effectively.
T he Nigerian Ministry of Health (MOH) and the National  Malaria Elimination Programme (NMEP) can play a key  Alao et al.
BMC Public Health (twenty twenty-five) twenty-five:three thousand seventy-nine  Page nine of ten role in targeting these groups to boost ITN usage across  all income levels.
Understanding and addressing both the knowledge  gaps and real-world barriers to using ITNs will enable  these programs to make a lasting difference.

One hundred eight thousand eighty-four  Malaria remains a leading global health challenge, impacting  over two hundred sixty-three million people across eighty-three countries in twenty twenty-three.
The World  Health Organization (WHO) African Region alone accounted for  two hundred forty-six million (ninety-four percent) malaria cases and five thousand, six hundred ninety zero zero (ninety-five percent) malaria deaths.
Nine percent of these deaths occurred in Nigeria, and the country  also accounted for twenty-seven percent of global malaria cases in twenty twenty-two [one, two].

This is an open access article under the CC BY license  ( http://creativecommons.org).
Historically, antimalarial therapy relied on drugs such as quino-  lines, tetracyclines, and sulfonamides [five].
However, widespread  resistance to monotherapies and older regimens led to a paradigm  shift in treatment strategies [six].
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recom-  mends AL as the first-line treatment of uncomplicated P. falciparum  malaria [eight].
Moreover, it is one of the most widely recommended  and used treatments across various African countries [nine–eleven].
Another challenge is the resistance to antimalarial  drugs [thirteen].
Currently, the standard treatment for uncomplicated P.falciparum
However, the clinical efficacy of antimalarial drugs  has been reduced due to drug-resistant strains of P. falciparum  [sixteen].
Between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty-two, ten studies conducted in the WHO  African Region revealed treatment failure exceeding ten percent with AL  [two].
These findings emphasize the need for the development  of new and effective antimalarial treatments [two , three].
The use of triple ACTs or non-artemisinin-based combination  therapies may be useful in such cases [three].
A fixed-dose combination (FDC)  of arterolane maleate-piperaquine phosphate (AMP) is proven to  effectively eliminate residual parasites [five, seventeen].
Moreover, its once daily dosing regimen improves patient adherence due to the reduction in pill burden [eighteen].
However, these  trials excluded patients from Nigeria [two, four, nineteen].

Blinding was not feasible due to differences in  dosing schedules between AMP and AL.
However, the use of ob-  jective parasitological endpoints helped mitigate the possible bias  due to open-label design.
The study was conducted at four sites in Nigeria (two sites each  in Osun State and Lagos State) between July twenty twenty-three and October  twenty twenty-four.

Randomization procedure and study interventions  A simple randomization method was employed using a balloting method at each site.
The simple balloting method was imple-mented with sealed, opaque, sequentially numbered envelopes to  maintain allocation concealment.
Site staff were not involved in  sequence generation.
To address potential site-specific differences,  we used site-stratified block randomization with variable, undisclosed block sizes.
Separate randomization lists were maintained  for each site.
Patients who  vomited within an hour of receiving a dose were withdrawn from  the study.

On Days three and twenty-eight, a total of eight mL venous blood was collected  for CBC, liver and renal function tests, and thick film preparation.
Capillary blood was obtained via finger prick for thick film microscopy on Days zero, three, seven, fourteen, twenty-eight, and forty-two.
The slides were examined at screening (Day zero) to assess eligibility  and determine parasite count.
On Days zero, three, seven, fourteen, twenty-eight, and forty-two, only  thick films were prepared and examined, following standard protocol [twenty].
Each thin film was fixed with methanol, and both thick  and thin films were stained with three percent Giemsa stain [twenty-one].
The key secondary endpoints included the proportion of patients with PCR-uncorrected ACPR on Day twenty-eight and fever clearance  time (FCT).

Safety results  One patient in the test group developed scabies, which was  deemed unrelated to the study treatment.
Minor AEs were re-  ported, but these AEs were self-limiting and did not necessitate  treatment discontinuation.
No severe AEs were observed during  the study.
The mean hemoglobin levels in the Test group increased from  baseline to Day three and were sustained till Day forty-two ( P  equals to zero.
A significant reduction in white  blood cell (WBC) count was noted in the Test group by Day forty-two  ( P  equals to zero.
Fifteen), while the WBC levels remained stable in the Com-  parator group from baseline to Day forty-two.
The PCR-corrected ACPR was consistent till Day  forty-two (one hundred percent), indicating sustained efficacy.
The PCR-uncorrected ACPR  on Days twenty-eight and forty-two, PCT, and FCT were comparable between both  treatment groups.
Both treatment groups also demonstrated signif-  icant hematological changes from baseline to Day forty-two.
In another study, Silva Pinto A et al.
Documented  late clinical failures in travelers returning from Luanda, Angola,  treated with AL [twenty-five].
These findings further highlight the variabil-  ity in treatment response and the potential for resistance devel-  opment.
Supporting this, Derbie A et al.
Confirmed the continued  effectiveness of AL in Africa but emphasized the need for region-  specific surveillance [twenty-six].
In Sudan, Mohamed AS et al.
Six percent treatment failure  rate with AL, partially attributed to non-adherence and improper  intake with fatty meals.
The study also stated that AL is becom-  ing less effective in Sudanese patients with uncomplicated malaria  [twenty-seven].
Additionally, one patient required  hospitalization due to incorrect dosing of AL [twenty-eight].
Therefore, AMP  can be an effective alternative to AL to improve treatment adher-  ence.
The results of our study also align with previous studies that  used a similar dosing of AMP.
The results of a study by Toure OA  et al.
Evaluating AMP once-daily versus AL twice daily in ten seventy-two  patients with uncomplicated P. falciparum infection, demonstrated  PCR-corrected ACPR of ninety-nine.
Seven percent in AMP and AL groups,  respectively, on Day twenty-eight.
A sustained efficacy of  greater than ninety-eight percent was noted in  both treatment groups on Day forty-two [four].
Similar results were observed in another multicenter, random-  ized clinical trial evaluating AMP versus AL.
This study reported  no treatment failures in the AMP group, while one treatment failure was reported in the AL group.
Additionally, they found no difference in median parasite and FCT between the two treatment  groups [seventeen].
A study in pediatric patients aged six months to twelve  years has also demonstrated similar results [thirteen].
The median PCT was found to be thirty hours in another  study [seventeen].
Together, these findings support the applicability and  reliability of AMP in adolescents and adults aged twelve-sixty-five years.
This study also demonstrated a favorable safety profile of AMP.
Although there were minor AEs reported in the study, they were  considered unlikely to be related to the study treatments.
These  findings support that AMP and AL have a similar safety profile.
Importantly, no patients developed clinically significant arrhyth-  mias, and AEs were generally resolved without sequelae.
Beyond QT  prolongation, the resistance potential of piperaquine also warrants  attention.
This option also eases the pill burden for  Nigerian patients with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria.
These  differences may limit the direct applicability of our findings to  urban malaria control.
Nonetheless, understanding treatment eff icacy in rural populations, who bear a disproportionately higher  malaria burden, remains highly relevant.

Introduction In twenty nineteen, pneumonia and malaria were estimated to cause  fourteen percent and seven.
One percent, respectively, of all childhood deaths world wide [one–three].
In malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan  Africa, a large proportion of acute febrile illnesses in children  are caused by malaria or pneumonia.
Central cyanosis, inability  to breastfeed/drink, vomiting everything, convulsions, leth argy, unconsciousness, or severe respiratory distress).
In  twenty thirteen, the WHO revised the classification of pneumonia, us ing the same signs, into two categories: non-severe and severe.
However, the trade-off for high sensitivity was poor specific ity: many children who do not have pneumonia are also cap tured by the case definition.
In sub-Saharan Africa, the  disease that is most likely to be misclassified as pneumonia is  Plasmodium falciparum malaria [eleven, sixteen].
At an average prev alence of twenty-four percent, malaria infection is common in the region  [seventeen] and frequently associated with respiratory symptoms  [twelve, eighteen, nineteen].
Thus, the extent to which pneumonia misclassification  occurs under the WHO criteria is uncertain [fifteen].
However,  data from chest X-rays present a possible avenue for gauging  this misclassification.
This analysis is restricted to three sites that were malaria-  endemic, i.
Kilifi, Kenya; Basse, The Gambia; and Bamako,  Mali.
No malaria was identified in South Africa, Thailand, or  Bangladesh and only two cases of malaria were identified in  Zambia.

OBJECTIVES We report estimates of global, national, and subnational CVD burden, including eighteen subdiseases and  twelve associated modifiable risk factors.
GBD twenty twenty-three estimated the population-level burden of diseases in two hundred four countries and territories  from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-three.
RESULTS CVDs were the leading cause of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) and deaths estimated in the GBD.
As of twenty twenty-three, there were four hundred thirty-seven million (ninety-five percent UI: four hundred one to four hundred sixty-five million) CVD DALYs globally, a one.
Four-fold increase from the number in  nineteen ninety of three hundred twenty million (two hundred ninety-two to three hundred forty-four million).

In the geographic cascade, disease  estimates were first generated at the global, or  highest, level.
These estimates were then used as  priors to generate estimates by GBD super-region.
This continued down the five levels of the GBD loca tion hierarchy, with the estimates for each level used  as the prior for the subsequent level.
RISK FACTOR ESTIMATION SUMMARY GBD estimated CVD burden attributable to twenty-eight risks.
Here we report aggregated risks to level two for clear  interpretability of results.
A  comparative risk assessment framework was utilized  to estimate the CVD burden from risk factors.
This  framework required convincing evidence of biologi cally plausible associations between risk exposure  and disease from epidemiological studies.
Most of the risks were evaluated  using the Burden of Proof methodology first intro duced in GBD twenty twenty-one to quantify the strength of evi dence.

Risk-attributable disease burden was calculated by multiplying the overall disease burden  by the PAF for each cause and associated risk.
Summary exposure values (SEVs) for each risk  were produced to allow for comparison across  risks.
The overall  SEV for a risk is the arithmetic mean of all the risk outcome-specific SEVs for that risk.
The calculation  of SEV includes all diseases caused by the risk factor,  not only CVD.
We report age-standardized SEVs on a  zero to one hundred scale, zero representing no exposure in the  population and one hundred indicating maximum exposure to  the risk.

DISCUSSION OVERVIEW AND KEY FINDINGS.
In twenty twenty-three, CVD was the leading cause of disease burden and deaths  worldwide (at level two).
The global burden of CVD is not declining.
Summary exposure values are a measure of  risk-weighted exposure in the population with a possible range of zero to one hundred.
Risk factor attribution varied considerably be tween regions.
For example, household air pollution was a larger cause of CVD in Oceania and SSA than other regions.
High alcohol use was a larger cause of  CVD in Eastern Europe than other regions.
High so dium consumption was a larger cause of CVD in East  Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Europe, and Oceania.
Given this kind of variation, disease burden estimates offer the opportunity to tailor local health  policies to target the most relevant risks.

Our findings emphasize that expo sure levels to these complex, intertwined risks  continue to rise even in the face of innovative ther apies.

Effective  policies are helping to reduce household air pollu tion, eliminate trans fat, and decrease access to to bacco.

POLICIES AND INTERVENTIONS TO ADDRESS CVD BURDEN.
Twenty-two, twenty twenty-five DECEMBER two, twenty twenty-five:twenty-one sixty-seven–twenty-two forty-three large proportion of people, contributing to large  global disparities in CVD.
The available  health care workforce trained to diagnose and treat  CVD and its risk factors remains limited.
Seventy-six In the current era, tobacco prevention has  been among the most effective policies for the  reduction of CVD burden.
Seventy-eight In comparison,  global efforts to reduce exposure to the harmful ef fects of alcohol have varied.
Installation of air pollution control tech nologies has been a successful strategy for reducing  ambient pollution in some locations such as China.
Eighty  Improvements in diet have been limited but  promising, with increasing numbers of countries  banning trans fats.
The effect of Mexico’s tax on  sugar-sweetened beverages remains unclear.
Eight thousand, one hundred eighty-two  Japan and the United Kingdom have adopted broad,  effective policies to reduce sodium consumption.
Eighty-three  Front-of-package labeling is being adopted in multi ple countries to provide consumers with information  on nutritional value.
Eighty-five LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE EFFORTS IN GLOBAL SURVEILLANCE.
Estimates from the GBD study were  limited by the quality and availability of input data,  particularly in data-sparse regions.
We report  country-level details on data availability for this  analysis in Supplemental Appendix one (Supplemental  Figure twenty-one, Supplemental Table twelve).
For  example, fifty of fifty-six countries with no cause-of-death  data for total CVD had available input data to  inform estimates of mean SBP.
In the  absence of direct data on CVD burden, robust statis tical models using covariates generated estimates.
Data on mediation of risk factors by  other risks and how that may vary between pop ulations remain limited.
There are also risk factors  not yet included in the GBD study, such as isolated  elevation in diastolic blood pressure.
IMPLICATIONS FOR HEALTH SYSTEMS AND PRIORITY SETTING.
Investment in cardiovascular health pol icies will be challenging in the current political and  economic climate.
Eighty-six Only a small  proportion of this funding was ever invested in non communicable diseases.
Eighty-seven and  reduce  out-of JACC VOL.
Taken together, this data suggests that, if current  trends continue, the Sustainable Development Goals  Target three.
Four of a one-third reduction in premature  mortality from non-communicable diseases between  twenty fifteen and twenty thirty is not likely to be met.
Policies  should also support the eradication of rheumatic  heart disease, which remains a persistent health  threat in the poorest countries.
Ambient air pollution and environmental lead expo sure remain serious health threats.
Effective health  systems and public health strategies exist to reduce  these risks.
Countries will need to adopt these stra tegies if they are to progress in achieving global goals  to reduce the burden of CVD.

The World Health Organization (WHO) highlights the heightened vulnerability of both mothers and neonates in malaria-endemic regions.
Study selection, data extraction, and methodological quality assessment were performed independently by two investigators.
From four hundred eighty-three studies identified, thirty-five studies comprising nine thousand, five hundred three neonates met the inclusion criteria.
The pooled prevalence of congenital malaria was twelve.
Two), with high heterogeneity (Itwo equals ninety-seven.
The average parasite count from neonates with congenital malaria was fifty-six.
Neonates with both malaria and septicaemia were four.
Subgroup analyses of maternal‑neonate pairings revealed maternal, placental, baby peripheral and cord blood malaria parasitaemia prevalences of twenty-five.
The average maternal age of parasitaemic babies was twenty-nine.
These findings emphasise the significant burden of congenital malaria in Nigeria, with potential adverse outcomes for newborn health.
CM remains a critical public health concern in endemic regions.
Enhanced surveillance and targeted interventions are imperative to reduce CM transmission and improve health outcomes.
Introduction Malaria continues to pose a major public health threat globally, with the highest burden concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa [one].
In twenty twenty-three, two hundred sixty-three million cases and five hundred ninety-seven thousand deaths were recorded across eighty-three countries.
The WHO African Region accounted for ninety-four  percent of cases and ninety-five  percent of deaths, highlighting a disproportionate burden [twenty-three].
Nigeria remains the most affected country, contributing up to twenty-five  percent of the malaria burden in sub-Saharan Africa [four].
Annually, the disease causes about one hundred ten million clinical cases, thirty  percent of hospital admissions, and sixty  percent of outpatient visits in the country [five].
Microscopy, though widely used, has limited sensitivity, particularly in neonates with low parasite densities.
The high prevalence of malaria in pregnancy in Nigeria raises concerns about the potential transmission of malaria to newborns [nineteen].
Studies investigating the prevalence of CM in Nigeria reveal substantial variability across regions, diagnostic methods, and study designs [nineteen].
Besides, there was no pooled national prevalence of CM for Nigeria in previous studies.
Factors such as maternal parasitaemia, placental infection, and suboptimal antenatal care have been implicated in the transmission risk [twenty-three twenty-four].
This study aims to systematically assess the prevalence of congenital malaria in Nigeria, synthesizing data from two decades of research.

The search targeted English-language articles published between January two thousand and December twenty twenty-four that examined congenital malaria in Nigeria.
Only full-text articles were included.
Following title and abstract screening, one hundred thirty-four studies were eligible for full-text assessment.

The increased vertical transmission of malaria is partly associated with the high susceptibility of women to malaria during pregnancy.
This systematic review aimed to assess the prevalence, characteristics, and treatment outcomes of congenital malaria in Nigeria.
Methods Twelve studies were included in this review.
The study was registered with PROSPERO and was conducted per PRSIMA-established guidelines.
Results The prevalence of congenital malaria in Nigeria ranged from as low as five.
Clinical manifestations were often non-specific, with fever being the most common symptom.
While treatment outcomes were generally positive, some studies reported complications and deaths.
By addressing these gaps, effective prevention and management strategies can be developed to reduce the burden of congenital malaria in Nigeria.

Children under five years old accounted for eighty percent of malaria deaths globally in twenty twenty-three [one].
Within this vulnerable cohort, congenital malaria represents a specific but often overlooked and misdiagnosed health challenge.
Congenital malaria presents unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges [four].
Many cases remain undiagnosed or untreated, leading to significant maternal and neonatal complications [fourteen].
Treatment of congenital malaria poses additional challenges, as anti-malarial regimens must balance efficacy with safety in this vulnerable age group.
Historically, older anti-malarial drugs, such as chloroquine, quinine, and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP), were commonly used.
The use of ACT in neonates has demonstrated superior outcomes, although safety and efficacy studies remain limited in this population.
Moreover, varying treatment practices and delays in administering effective therapies further compound the risks of poor neonatal outcomes [sixteen].
The protocol detailed the research question, objectives, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the methodological approach for this review.
The search was limited to English-language articles published from the inception of each database (e.
PubMed from nineteen forty, Scopus from two thousand four) to June twenty twenty-four.
Full-text articles of potentially eligible studies were then reviewed.
Any discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer (EK).
Quality assessment The quality of the included studies was evaluated using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) framework.
The CASP appraisal provided a structured approach to assessing the methodological rigor and overall reliability of the research.
Supplementary file one.
Data synthesis A narrative synthesis was used to summarize key findings, including prevalence, clinical characteristics, and treatment outcomes.
Results Study characteristics A total of one hundred sixty-two studies were identified through the search.
After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, twelve studies [eighteen–twenty-nine] were retained for the final analysis (Fig.
The total sample size across all the studies is four thousand, five hundred ten (see Table one).
The geographic scope of the studies spans multiple regions across Nigeria.
The Southwest region (highest number of studies) includes Ogun State (Sagamu), Lagos State, and Osun State (Ile-Ife).
The Northwest region is represented by Sokoto and Kaduna State (Zaria), while the North Central region features Abuja (FCT) and Plateau State (Jos).
Additionally, the Southeast region includes Anambra State (Awka) and Delta State (Eku).

However, it is important to contextualize these findings within the studied periods, as the treatment of malaria in Nigeria has evolved over time.
Studies have reported a wide range of prevalence rates, which highlight the impact of local malaria endemicity and diagnostic practices.
[nineteen] documented an average prevalence rate of five.
One percent in a multi-centre study conducted across three Nigerian states: Oyo, Kwara, and Kaduna, which represent different geopolitical zones.
In contrast, Runsewe-Abiodun et al.

Four percent in Sagamu, Ogun State.
[twenty] reported an even higher prevalence of forty-six.
Seven percent in Ile-Ife, Osun State.
Similarly, a study by Okechukwu et al.

Six percent in Abuja, in the Northcentral region.
Studies from the northern regions of Nigeria also show varying prevalence rates.
[twenty-three] recorded a striking prevalence of ninety-six.
Additionally, Diala et al.
[twenty-seven] reported a prevalence of five.
Three percent in Jos, Plateau State.
Other studies, such as Mukhtar et al.
[twenty-one] in Lagos and Hyacinth et al.
[twenty-six] in Jos, Plateau State, reported lower prevalence rates of thirteen.
However, Hyacinth et al.
[twenty-three] reported an equal number of male and female participants, unlike the other studies, which documented unequal male-to-female ratios.
This variability highlights demographic differences across study populations.
The clinical presentations of congenital malaria were largely non-specific, but certain patterns emerged.
Fever was the most consistently reported symptom, appearing in every case reported [nineteen, twenty-three, twenty-eight].
Across the studies that documented clinical features, fever was universally observed.
Poor feeding was another common clinical feature, identified in seventy-five percent of the reviewed studies [eighteen–twenty, eighteen–twenty].
Convulsions and cyanosis were each observed in seventeen percent of the studies [eighteen, twenty-four, twenty-six, twenty-seven], and hypothermia was similarly noted in seventeen percent [twenty, twenty-eight].
Excessive crying was also reported in seventeen percent of the studies [twenty-four, twenty-seven].
Less common symptoms included umbilical cord discharge, skin rashes, and oliguria, which were sporadically noted across the studies.
It is worth mentioning that Mukhtar et al.
Did not provide details about the clinical symptoms observed in their neonatal subjects [twenty-two, twenty-nine].
The choice of treatment was influenced by both the timing of the studies and the prevailing malaria treatment protocols.
For example, SP was employed in studies performed during a period when ACT had not yet been universally adopted [nineteen, twenty, twenty-nine].
Use of amodiaquine and quinine Amodiaquine, often used in combination with artesunate, was frequently used [twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-nine].
Quinine, administered through various routes, was used in the treatment of severe malaria cases.
It was still employed particularly before intravenous artesunate became more widely available [twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-eight].
In the study by Nwaneli et al.
ACT was also used in the study by Onankpa et al.
[twenty-three], consistent with the more recent guidelines from the WHO, which recommended ACT as the first-line treatment for uncomplicated malaria.
For instance, in the studies by Runsewe-Abiodun et al.
[twenty] and Obiajunwa et al.
[twenty-one], some patients did not receive any treatment, with six and ten untreated patients, respectively.
The study by Mukhtar et al.
[twenty-two] also involved patients who were monitored without therapeutic intervention, with follow-up extending to twenty-eight days.
These instances highlight gaps in treatment delivery, which were not aligned with malaria treatment guidelines at the time.

For example, in the study by Falade et al.
Although this approach reflected earlier treatment protocols, it likely led to suboptimal outcomes due to the development of chloroquine resistance.
In more recent studies, including that of Nwaneli et al.
In studies that followed the most current guidelines at the time, such as those that incorporated ACT, treatment success was particularly high.
For example, the study by Onankpa et al.
This is consistent with the broader adoption of ACT as a first-line treatment for uncomplicated malaria in line with updated guidelines.
In earlier studies that adhered to older treatment protocols, chloroquine was still widely used, with studies by Falade et al.
[nineteen] and Obiajunwa et al.
[twenty] showing high rates of parasitological cure and clinical improvement.
However, the effectiveness of chloroquine has been compromised over time due to the emergence of chloroquine-resistant strains of P. falciparum.
In instances where chloroquine was insufficient, other medications such as SP and quinine were successfully employed, ensuring positive outcomes.
For example, the studies by Runsewe-Abiodun et al.
[eighteen] and Okechukwu et al.

Complications and adverse outcomes Out of the twelve studies analysed, three [twenty, twenty-one, twenty-six] reported deaths attributable to congenital malaria.
Notably, in the study by Runsewe-Abiodun et al.
The treatments administered included chloroquine for fifty infants, SP) for one infant, and six neonates received no treatment at all.
Similarly, in the study by Hyacinth et al.
Congenital malaria was directly linked to neonatal deaths, though details on other potential contributing conditions were not specified [twenty-six].
The treatment regimens used included amodiaquine for twenty infants, quinine for three, and a combination of amodiaquine and quinine for one infant.
[twenty-three] highlighted a more complex scenario.
In contrast, the remaining studies reported no complications or fatalities directly attributable to congenital malaria.
Studies did not document any severe adverse outcomes [nineteen, twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-four, twenty-five, twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine].
Even in the case documented by Nwaneli et al.
Where the infant initially experienced seizures and opisthotonic posture, follow-up after one year revealed no lasting neurologic deficits [twenty-nine].
Discussion This review provides an analysis of congenital malaria in neonates, examining twelve studies across various regions in Nigeria.
In Nigeria, prevalence rates have ranged from as low as five.
One percent in a multi-center study across Oyo, Kwara, and Kaduna states [nineteen] to as high as ninety-six.
Three percent in Sokoto, reflecting the severe endemicity of malaria in this region [twenty-three].
These discrepancies mirror the regional malaria transmission intensity, which is a common pattern observed worldwide.
The prevalence rate of twenty-eight.
Six percent in Abuja [twenty-two] suggests that even in regions with better healthcare facilities, congenital malaria remains a significant concern.
On the other hand, regions with lower prevalence should focus on maintaining and enhancing existing malaria control programmes.
The variability in prevalence rates also emphasizes the diagnostic challenges of congenital malaria.
The non-specific nature of congenital malaria symptoms, which often overlap with those of other neonatal conditions, complicates early diagnosis.
Fever emerged as the most consistently reported symptom, corroborating previous studies [thirty-one, thirty-two].
The frequent occurrence of poor feeding, jaundice, and hepatomegaly further highlights the complex clinical spectrum of the disease.
This underscores the need for heightened clinical suspicion and early recognition, which can lead to prompt management and better outcomes [thirty-three, thirty-four].
Early and accurate diagnosis of congenital malaria is crucial, as it allows for timely intervention that can prevent severe complications.
However, the recurring use of chloroquine in several studies points to its historical prominence as a frontline anti-malarial drug.
The diverse treatment approaches observed across these studies have significant clinical implications.
This indicates the need for ongoing education and resources to support healthcare providers in transitioning to more effective treatment options.
While chloroquine remains effective in some contexts, the increasing prevalence of resistance necessitates a more widespread adoption of ACT.
Additionally, quinine and other drugs, while useful in some cases, should be evaluated against current resistance patterns and safety profiles.
Although treatment success rates were generally high across the studies, some did report complications and adverse outcomes, including fatalities.
Three of the twelve studies reviewed reported deaths attributable to congenital malaria, which underscores the severity of the condition in neonates.
This reinforces the need for comprehensive care that addresses both the malaria and its potential complications.
Limitations of review The studies used various methodologies, including different diagnostic criteria and treatment approaches.
This variability makes it difficult to directly compare results and draw definitive conclusions.
Moreover, the review primarily focused on treatment success rates and immediate complications.
It would be beneficial to understand the long-term health outcomes of neonates who had congenital malaria.
Conclusion This systematic review analysed the prevalence, characteristics, and treatment outcomes of congenital malaria in Nigeria.
Sokoto recorded a prevalence rate as high as ninety-six.
Three percent, while Oyo, Kwara, and Kaduna states reported a lower rate of five.
These disparities shows the need for targeted interventions in high-burden areas.
The clinical presentation of congenital malaria was complex and often non-specific, with fever being the most common symptom.
This highlights the challenge of early diagnosis and the importance of a high index of suspicion among healthcare providers.
A variety of antimalarial drugs were employed in treatment, with varying degrees of success.
Additionally, investigating adherence-enhancing interventions is crucial for optimizing malaria treatment.
It is important to note that the studies included in this review employed diverse methodologies, making direct comparisons challenging.
Moreover, the focus on treatment success rates and immediate complications limits the understanding of long-term health outcomes.
