Malaria not only impacts health but also affects Nigeria’s economic development and productivity.
The disease is responsible for millions of missed workdays and school absences annually, resulting in a loss of economic productivity.
It is estimated that malaria costs the Nigerian economy more than one dollar.
One billion annually in healthcare expenses and loss of productivity [three].
This remarkable success provides valuable lessons that can guide Nigeria’s approach to eradicating malaria.
By analysing Egypt’s strategies, this paper aims to identify actionable interventions that can be tailored to Nigeria’s context.
World War II exacerbated the situation, with over three million reported cases due to the spread of Anopheles arabiensis.
The construction of the Aswan Dam in nineteen sixty-nine introduced a new malaria challenge, as the dam created ideal breeding conditions for mosquitoes.
To counter this, Egypt collaborated with Sudan on a rigorous vector control and surveillance project [six].
These efforts helped control malaria, and by two thousand one, the disease was largely under control, with the focus shifting to prevent outbreaks.
In twenty twenty-four, Egypt achieved a historic milestone by being declared malaria-free, earning certification from the World Health Organization (WHO).
This made Egypt the third country in the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region to reach this status [seven].
These coordinated global efforts aim to eliminate malaria through systematic and widespread intervention strategies.
These systems supported early detection and rapid response to malaria cases.
Vector control measures were another cornerstone of Egypt’s strategy.
These aimed to reduce human-to-mosquito contact, a critical step in interrupting malaria transmission.
Public awareness and education also played a pivotal role.
Community sensitization campaigns were conducted to educate the public about malaria transmission, symptoms, and prevention.
These initiatives empowered individuals to take proactive steps, such as using preventive tools and seeking early treatment [ten].
This accessibility ensured that individuals could receive timely care, thereby reducing the disease burden [ten].
Collaboration with international organizations, such as the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Global Fund further bolstered Egypt’s efforts.
These partnerships provided critical resources, technical support, and funding essential for implementing effective malaria control strategies [eleven].
Finally, policy implementation and governmental commitment were instrumental in sustaining malaria eradication initiatives.
The establishment of the National Malaria Control Programme ensured sustained political and financial commitment.
First, China’s malaria elimination success was driven by strong governmental leadership that unified multiple sectors under a coordinated framework.
Strategic decisions were based on scientific evidence, epidemiological data, and local conditions.
National programmes provided clear technical guidance and resource allocation to targeted regions.
Sustained financial commitment, including one Naira.
Thirty-eight billion from government and global partners, demonstrated the countries determination to end malaria [thirteen, fourteen].
Real-time reporting through digital platforms and the one–three–seven strategy enhanced response speed and accuracy [fifteen].
A robust diagnostic network ensures quality control across health facilities.
Since twenty sixteen, anti-malarial surveillance has strengthened efforts, including drug resistance monitoring and patient follow-up [thirteen].
International partnerships with WHO, the Global Fund, and others provided technical and financial support.
Cross-border cooperation further reduced malaria, especially along the China–Myanmar border.
These efforts strengthened both national and global malaria control [thirteen, sixteen].
Strategies such as case investigation, vector surveillance, and expert oversight were implemented at the national and provincial levels.
Similarly, Argentina’s journey to eliminate malaria focused on sustained efforts in the northern regions where the disease burden was highest.
A national surveillance system supported by decentralized labs and consistent domestic funding ensured sustained efforts despite reduced external aid.
The resilience of the VC network and its grassroots approach were central to achieving a ninety-five percent reduction in malaria cases between nineteen eighty-one and nineteen ninety-five.
Nigeria, as a country with a high malaria burden, can adapt Egypt’s strategies to improve its malaria control outcomes.
Similarly, while Nigeria has malaria control strategies in place, the uptake of preventive measures, such as LLINs and IRS has been suboptimal.
These efforts should be complemented by enhanced healthcare infrastructure to ensure the effective delivery of malaria interventions.
To overcome these barriers, funding initiatives must prioritize free malaria diagnosis and treatment.
A lack of political will and leadership remains a major obstacle to sustained and coordinated interventions.
This coordinated approach will foster a robust system capable of driving sustainable malaria control and eventual eradication [thirty-six, thirty-seven].
Strengthening these systems is essential for achieving malaria elimination in the country.
However, the widespread use of ACT without prior diagnosis poses significant challenges.
This hesitancy, often fueled by socio-cultural, religious, and political factors [forty-two], remains a significant barrier to achieving widespread immunity.
Prioritizing public education on the benefits of the vaccine and other malaria control strategies will be pivotal in Nigeria’s fight against malaria.
Limitations This study is primarily a desk-based narrative review that draws on secondary data and published reports.
The selection of case studies, though informed by WHO documentation on malaria elimination, may also introduce regional bias.

Malaria parasites, which kill nearly six hundred thousand people a year, mostly children, are spread by female mosquitoes when they drink blood.
Current efforts aim to kill mosquitoes with insecticide rather than curing them of malaria.
But a team at Harvard University has found a pair of drugs which can successfully rid the insects of malaria when absorbed through their legs.
Coating bed nets in the drug cocktail is the long-term aim.
Sleeping under a bed net has been one of the most successful ways of preventing malaria as the main malaria-spreading mosquitoes hunt at night.
Vaccines to protect children living in high-risk malaria areas are also recommended.
Nets are both a physical barrier and also contain insecticides which kill mosquitoes that land on them.
But mosquitoes have become resistant to insecticide in many countries so the chemicals no longer kill the insects as effectively as they used to.
However, she says that approach is "no longer cutting it".
They took a large library of potential drugs and narrowed it down to a shortlist of twenty-two.
These were tested when female mosquitoes were given a blood-meal contaminated with malaria.
In their article in Nature, the scientists describe two highly effective drugs that killed one hundred percent of the parasites.
The drugs were tested on material similar to bed nets.
"I think this is a really exciting approach, because it's a totally new way of targeting mosquitoes themselves.
The effect of the drugs lasts for a year on the nets, potentially making it a cheap and long-lasting alternative to insecticide, the researchers say.
This approach has been proven in the laboratory.
The next stage is already planned in Ethiopia to see if the anti-malarial bed nets are effective in the real world.
It will take at least six years before all the studies are completed to know if this approach will work.
But the vision is to have bed nets treated with both anti-malaria drugs and insecticide so that if one approach doesn't work, then the other will.

Here Mahlatse Gallens reports from northern South Africa on how the battle to tackle malaria is going.
Armed for battle against one of Africa's deadly diseases, they brandish canisters filled with the deadly insecticide DDT.
When sprayed properly it can keep mosquitoes carrying malaria at bay for more than eight months.
Their success is pinned on educational drives that include radio talk shows, posters and brochures in local languages and door-to-door campaigning.
Zatley Sekgobela, the man in charge, says they have an intensive three-week training programme to ensure they do not get the spraying wrong.
"We want them to deposit three grams per square km of insecticide.
When they spray it must be forty-five cm from the wall.
We don't want to waste or spill the insecticide.
Welcome  Lydia Mhlongo is more than happy to open her doors to them.
Just last year she had to nurse her son and his friend to recovery after they fell ill with cerebral malaria.
Primary health care is at the core of the malaria programme.
In Limpopo alone, four hundred eighty clinics equipped with diagnostic tests and combination drugs for those testing positive have been built.
For people like Lydia, indoor spraying is their only weapon against the disease.
Unemployment is very high here and they cannot afford repellents or insecticide-treated nets.
The South African government is not providing nets at all but has opted for indoor residual spraying.
History  South Africa had stopped using DDT in nineteen ninety-six.
Until then the total number of malaria cases was below ten thousand and there were seldom more than thirty deaths per year.
But in two thousand, the country saw malaria cases skyrocket to sixty-five thousand and four hundred fifty-eight people were killed.
Provincial health minister Seaparo Sekwati defends the use of DDT, saying it saves lives.
"We are going to continue using DDT as it has worked and has worked for those developed countries in the past.
Last year only eighty-nine deaths were recorded.
But the disease can never be fully eradicated without neighbouring countries also jacking up their malaria control programmes.
South Africa is also providing resources and technical training to Zimbabwe's southern Matabeleland province and assistance to Angola.
Richard Tren, Director of Africa Fighting Malaria, describes the malaria programme as one of the best in the region.
He attributes this success to the fact that it is well funded and because the government has the freedom to decide on how to intervene.
"Countries like Tanzania, and Kenya are very reliant on donors.
That means they basically have to do what the donors say they must do.
Donors shy away from interventions like indoor residual spraying.
"They really force them to use insecticide-treated nets.
That on its own is not going to control malaria or meet the MDGs.
But the key is to sustain current projects.
The West African nation accounts for almost a third of those who die from malaria each year.
The roll-out started in two of the worst-affected states - Bayelsa and Kebbi – and the plan is to expand it to the rest of the country by next year.

Globally, there are approximately two hundred forty-nine million reported cases of malaria, leading  to six hundred eight thousand deaths (WHO twenty twenty-three).
Nigeria, in particular,  contributes significantly, up to twenty-seven percent of all malaria cases worldwide (WHO twenty twenty-three).
Effective malaria case management is a crucial and widely used method for  malaria control.
Chloroquine (CQ), introduced in the mid-nineteen fortys, was once the cornerstone of  malaria treatment due to its effectiveness, safety, and affordability.
Twenty twenty-one), and prompted a global review of malaria treatment  policies.
They function by disrupting the digestion of hemoglobin during the blood stages  of the malaria parasite’s life cycle (Combrinck et al.
These mutations alter the parasite’s susceptibility to CQ and other antimalarials  (Roux et al.
Pfcrt and pfmdrone are vital transporters within Plasmodium,  serving dual roles as mediators of drug resistance and as drug targets.
Initially, the mutation in  pfcrt and pfmdrone was recognized for their involvement in conferring chloroquine  resistance (Fidock et al.
Nineteen ninety), but are now known to influence  parasite’s susceptibility to numerous contemporary antimalarial drugs (Cheruiyot  et al.
The emergence of parasite resistance to artemisinin derivatives and partner drugs  in ACT poses a significant threat to malaria control.

Lagos is located at six.
Seven thousand, five hundred degree East in the South-Western region of Nigeria, with an altitude of forty m (one hundred thirty-one feet).
It shares  its borders with Ogun State to the north and east, the Republic of Benin to the west,  and the Atlantic Ocean to the south (Fig.
The city has a coastline of approxi mately one hundred eighty km, characterized by lagoons, creeks, and swamps.
These water bodies  are separated from the open sea by a sandy land strip, varying in width from two to  sixteen km.
Lagos experiences a tropical climate, with most months marked by signifi cant rainfall and a short dry season.
The area is holoendemic for malaria, with a  mean temperature of twenty-six.

However, the inverse relationship between education  and reported net use contrasts with the positive associa tion between education and awareness.

T he study’s findings have several practical implications.
Tailored messaging that addresses perceptions,  convenience, and alternative protection strategies may  enhance ITN adherence.
Second, increasing malaria  prevention awareness through education is critical, but  insufficient alone to ensure net use.
T here are several reasons why media exposure was not  significantly associated with treatment-seeking behaviour  in this study.
Even when  media campaigns are widespread, the content may not  resonate with local values, beliefs, or language, limit ing its effectiveness.
Another reason could be the struc tural barriers to healthcare access.
In many rural areas,  these barriers can be just as significant as awareness, if  not more so.
Lastly, passive exposure to media without  active engagement or trust in the messaging may also  contribute to the lack of significant impact.
This underscores the importance  of increasing media exposure and ensuring that messages  are engaging, credible, and trusted by the target audience.
T his study has limitations.
The wealth index, while a standard proxy for  socioeconomic status, may not capture all dimensions  of economic variation.
Furthermore, media exposure  was broadly defined and did not assess content, message  quality, or comprehension.
Additionally, several unmeasured confounders may  influence the observed relationships.
For example, differ ences in local malaria transmission intensity could affect  both ITN use and treatment-seeking behaviour.
In addition, the media exposure analysis, with a sample  size of n  equals to eight hundred ninety-three, is smaller than the other analyses in this  study.
As such, its findings should be interpreted with  caution, and the conclusions drawn from this smaller  sample may not be as generalizable.
Further research  with larger sample sizes is needed to confirm these find ings.
Future research should employ longitudinal designs to  capture temporal changes in malaria prevention behav iours more effectively.
T he Nigerian Ministry of Health (MOH) and the National  Malaria Elimination Programme (NMEP) can play a key  Alao et al.
BMC Public Health (twenty twenty-five) twenty-five:three thousand seventy-nine  Page nine of ten role in targeting these groups to boost ITN usage across  all income levels.
Understanding and addressing both the knowledge  gaps and real-world barriers to using ITNs will enable  these programs to make a lasting difference.

One hundred eight thousand eighty-four  Malaria remains a leading global health challenge, impacting  over two hundred sixty-three million people across eighty-three countries in twenty twenty-three.
The World  Health Organization (WHO) African Region alone accounted for  two hundred forty-six million (ninety-four percent) malaria cases and five thousand, six hundred ninety zero zero (ninety-five percent) malaria deaths.
Nine percent of these deaths occurred in Nigeria, and the country  also accounted for twenty-seven percent of global malaria cases in twenty twenty-two [one, two].

Historically, antimalarial therapy relied on drugs such as quino-  lines, tetracyclines, and sulfonamides [five].
However, widespread  resistance to monotherapies and older regimens led to a paradigm  shift in treatment strategies [six].
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recom-  mends AL as the first-line treatment of uncomplicated P. falciparum  malaria [eight].
Moreover, it is one of the most widely recommended  and used treatments across various African countries [nine–eleven].
Another challenge is the resistance to antimalarial  drugs [thirteen].
Currently, the standard treatment for uncomplicated P.falciparum
However, the clinical efficacy of antimalarial drugs  has been reduced due to drug-resistant strains of P. falciparum  [sixteen].
Between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty-two, ten studies conducted in the WHO  African Region revealed treatment failure exceeding ten percent with AL  [two].
These findings emphasize the need for the development  of new and effective antimalarial treatments [two , three].
The use of triple ACTs or non-artemisinin-based combination  therapies may be useful in such cases [three].
A fixed-dose combination (FDC)  of arterolane maleate-piperaquine phosphate (AMP) is proven to  effectively eliminate residual parasites [five, seventeen].
Moreover, its once daily dosing regimen improves patient adherence due to the reduction in pill burden [eighteen].
However, these  trials excluded patients from Nigeria [two, four, nineteen].
Falciparum malaria in adolescent and adult Nigerian patients.
Falciparum malaria.
Blinding was not feasible due to differences in  dosing schedules between AMP and AL.
However, the use of ob-  jective parasitological endpoints helped mitigate the possible bias  due to open-label design.
The study was conducted at four sites in Nigeria (two sites each  in Osun State and Lagos State) between July twenty twenty-three and October  twenty twenty-four.

Randomization procedure and study interventions  A simple randomization method was employed using a balloting method at each site.
The simple balloting method was imple-mented with sealed, opaque, sequentially numbered envelopes to  maintain allocation concealment.
Site staff were not involved in  sequence generation.
To address potential site-specific differences,  we used site-stratified block randomization with variable, undisclosed block sizes.
Separate randomization lists were maintained  for each site.
Patients who  vomited within an hour of receiving a dose were withdrawn from  the study.

On Days three and twenty-eight, a total of eight mL venous blood was collected  for CBC, liver and renal function tests, and thick film preparation.
Capillary blood was obtained via finger prick for thick film microscopy on Days zero, three, seven, fourteen, twenty-eight, and forty-two.
The slides were examined at screening (Day zero) to assess eligibility  and determine parasite count.
On Days zero, three, seven, fourteen, twenty-eight, and forty-two, only  thick films were prepared and examined, following standard protocol [twenty].
Each thin film was fixed with methanol, and both thick  and thin films were stained with three percent Giemsa stain [twenty-one].
The key secondary endpoints included the proportion of patients with PCR-uncorrected ACPR on Day twenty-eight and fever clearance  time (FCT).
Safety assessments were  also conducted during the study.
AEs were coded us-ing the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version twenty-seven.
Zero, graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria  for AEs (CTCAE) version five.
Zero, and causality of all AEs was assessed  by investigators using WHO-Uppsala Monitoring Centre criteria.

Safety results  One patient in the test group developed scabies, which was  deemed unrelated to the study treatment.
Minor AEs were re-  ported, but these AEs were self-limiting and did not necessitate  treatment discontinuation.
No severe AEs were observed during  the study.
The mean hemoglobin levels in the Test group increased from  baseline to Day three and were sustained till Day forty-two ( P  equals to zero.
A significant reduction in white  blood cell (WBC) count was noted in the Test group by Day forty-two  ( P  equals to zero.
Fifteen), while the WBC levels remained stable in the Com-  parator group from baseline to Day forty-two.
The PCR-corrected ACPR was consistent till Day  forty-two (one hundred percent), indicating sustained efficacy.
The PCR-uncorrected ACPR  on Days twenty-eight and forty-two, PCT, and FCT were comparable between both  treatment groups.
Both treatment groups also demonstrated signif-  icant hematological changes from baseline to Day forty-two.
In another study, Silva Pinto A et al.
Documented  late clinical failures in travelers returning from Luanda, Angola,  treated with AL [twenty-five].
These findings further highlight the variabil-  ity in treatment response and the potential for resistance devel-  opment.
Supporting this, Derbie A et al.
Confirmed the continued  effectiveness of AL in Africa but emphasized the need for region-  specific surveillance [twenty-six].
In Sudan, Mohamed AS et al.
Six percent treatment failure  rate with AL, partially attributed to non-adherence and improper  intake with fatty meals.
The study also stated that AL is becom-  ing less effective in Sudanese patients with uncomplicated malaria  [twenty-seven].
Additionally, one patient required  hospitalization due to incorrect dosing of AL [twenty-eight].
Therefore, AMP  can be an effective alternative to AL to improve treatment adher-  ence.
The results of our study also align with previous studies that  used a similar dosing of AMP.
The results of a study by Toure OA  et al.
Evaluating AMP once-daily versus AL twice daily in ten seventy-two  patients with uncomplicated P. falciparum infection, demonstrated  PCR-corrected ACPR of ninety-nine.
Seven percent in AMP and AL groups,  respectively, on Day twenty-eight.
A sustained efficacy of  greater than ninety-eight percent was noted in  both treatment groups on Day forty-two [four].
Similar results were observed in another multicenter, random-  ized clinical trial evaluating AMP versus AL.
This study reported  no treatment failures in the AMP group, while one treatment failure was reported in the AL group.
Additionally, they found no difference in median parasite and FCT between the two treatment  groups [seventeen].
A study in pediatric patients aged six months to twelve  years has also demonstrated similar results [thirteen].
The median PCT was found to be thirty hours in another  study [seventeen].
Together, these findings support the applicability and  reliability of AMP in adolescents and adults aged twelve-sixty-five years.
This study also demonstrated a favorable safety profile of AMP.
Although there were minor AEs reported in the study, they were  considered unlikely to be related to the study treatments.
These  findings support that AMP and AL have a similar safety profile.
Importantly, no patients developed clinically significant arrhyth-  mias, and AEs were generally resolved without sequelae.
Beyond QT  prolongation, the resistance potential of piperaquine also warrants  attention.
This option also eases the pill burden for Nigerian patients with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria.
These  differences may limit the direct applicability of our findings to  urban malaria control.
Nonetheless, understanding treatment eff icacy in rural populations, who bear a disproportionately higher  malaria burden, remains highly relevant.

Introduction In twenty nineteen, pneumonia and malaria were estimated to cause  fourteen percent and seven.
One percent, respectively, of all childhood deaths world wide [one–three].
In malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan  Africa, a large proportion of acute febrile illnesses in children  are caused by malaria or pneumonia.
Central cyanosis, inability  to breastfeed/drink, vomiting everything, convulsions, leth argy, unconsciousness, or severe respiratory distress).
In twenty thirteen, the WHO revised the classification of pneumonia, us ing the same signs, into two categories: non-severe and severe.
However, the trade-off for high sensitivity was poor specific ity: many children who do not have pneumonia are also cap tured by the case definition.
In sub-Saharan Africa, the  disease that is most likely to be misclassified as pneumonia is  Plasmodium falciparum malaria [eleven, sixteen].
At an average prev alence of twenty-four percent, malaria infection is common in the region  [seventeen] and frequently associated with respiratory symptoms  [twelve, eighteen, nineteen].
Thus, the extent to which pneumonia misclassification  occurs under the WHO criteria is uncertain [fifteen].
However,  data from chest X-rays present a possible avenue for gauging  this misclassification.
This analysis is restricted to three sites that were malaria-  endemic, i.
Kilifi, Kenya; Basse, The Gambia; and Bamako,  Mali.
No malaria was identified in South Africa, Thailand, or  Bangladesh and only two cases of malaria were identified in  Zambia.

Discussion Among clinically diagnosed WHO pneumonia cases from the  PERCH study, we estimated that ninety-seven.
Five percent were true instances  of pneumonia and two.
Five percent were misclassified.
This high PPV is  largely attributable to the low prevalence of malaria parasi taemia in the PERCH WHO pneumonia cases.
Indeed, in set tings that are more representative of malaria endemicity, we  estimate the PPV to be in the region of seventy percent.
This prediction is sup ported by data from Kilifi, Kenya, where surveillance data on  both malaria parasitaemia and pneumonia are available.
Our model predicts a de cline of forty percent in clinical pneumonia cases (thirty percent due to mis classified malaria and ten percent directly attributable to malaria).
Thus, the decline in clinical pneumonia in Kilifi is largely  explained by the reduction in malaria.
The assumptions that underlie our estimation of PPV in  PERCH merit evaluation.
By using chest radiography as our  reference standard, we assumed that CXR is one hundred percent specific.

In the geographic cascade, disease  estimates were first generated at the global, or  highest, level.
These estimates were then used as  priors to generate estimates by GBD super-region.
This continued down the five levels of the GBD loca tion hierarchy, with the estimates for each level used  as the prior for the subsequent level.
RISK FACTOR ESTIMATION SUMMARY GBD estimated CVD burden attributable to twenty-eight risks.
Here we report aggregated risks to level two for clear  interpretability of results.
A  comparative risk assessment framework was utilized  to estimate the CVD burden from risk factors.
This  framework required convincing evidence of biologi cally plausible associations between risk exposure  and disease from epidemiological studies.
Most of the risks were evaluated  using the Burden of Proof methodology first intro duced in GBD twenty twenty-one to quantify the strength of evi dence.

Risk-attributable disease burden was calculated by multiplying the overall disease burden  by the PAF for each cause and associated risk.
Summary exposure values (SEVs) for each risk  were produced to allow for comparison across  risks.
The overall  SEV for a risk is the arithmetic mean of all the risk outcome-specific SEVs for that risk.
The calculation  of SEV includes all diseases caused by the risk factor,  not only CVD.
We report age-standardized SEVs on a  zero to one hundred scale, zero representing no exposure in the  population and one hundred indicating maximum exposure to  the risk.

DISCUSSION OVERVIEW AND KEY FINDINGS.
In twenty twenty-three, CVD was the leading cause of disease burden and deaths  worldwide (at level two).
The global burden of CVD is not declining.
Summary exposure values are a measure of  risk-weighted exposure in the population with a possible range of zero to one hundred.
Risk factor attribution varied considerably be tween regions.
For example, household air pollution was a larger cause of CVD in Oceania and SSA than other regions.
High alcohol use was a larger cause of  CVD in Eastern Europe than other regions.
High so dium consumption was a larger cause of CVD in East  Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Europe, and Oceania.
Given this kind of variation, disease burden estimates offer the opportunity to tailor local health  policies to target the most relevant risks.

POLICIES AND INTERVENTIONS TO ADDRESS CVD BURDEN.
Twenty-two, twenty twenty-five DECEMBER two, twenty twenty-five:twenty-one sixty-seven–twenty-two forty-three large proportion of people, contributing to large  global disparities in CVD.
The available  health care workforce trained to diagnose and treat  CVD and its risk factors remains limited.
Seventy-six In the current era, tobacco prevention has  been among the most effective policies for the  reduction of CVD burden.
Seventy-eight In comparison,  global efforts to reduce exposure to the harmful ef fects of alcohol have varied.
Installation of air pollution control tech nologies has been a successful strategy for reducing  ambient pollution in some locations such as China.
Eighty  Improvements in diet have been limited but  promising, with increasing numbers of countries  banning trans fats.
The effect of Mexico’s tax on  sugar-sweetened beverages remains unclear.
Eight thousand, one hundred eighty-two  Japan and the United Kingdom have adopted broad,  effective policies to reduce sodium consumption.
Eighty-three  Front-of-package labeling is being adopted in multi ple countries to provide consumers with information  on nutritional value.
Eighty-five LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE EFFORTS IN GLOBAL SURVEILLANCE.
Estimates from the GBD study were  limited by the quality and availability of input data,  particularly in data-sparse regions.
We report  country-level details on data availability for this  analysis in Supplemental Appendix one (Supplemental  Figure twenty-one, Supplemental Table twelve).
For  example, fifty of fifty-six countries with no cause-of-death  data for total CVD had available input data to  inform estimates of mean SBP.
In the  absence of direct data on CVD burden, robust statis tical models using covariates generated estimates.
Data on mediation of risk factors by  other risks and how that may vary between pop ulations remain limited.
There are also risk factors  not yet included in the GBD study, such as isolated  elevation in diastolic blood pressure.
IMPLICATIONS FOR HEALTH SYSTEMS AND PRIORITY SETTING.
Investment in cardiovascular health pol icies will be challenging in the current political and  economic climate.
Eighty-six Only a small  proportion of this funding was ever invested in non communicable diseases.
Eighty-seven and  reduce  out-of JACC VOL.
Taken together, this data suggests that, if current  trends continue, the Sustainable Development Goals  Target three.
Four of a one-third reduction in premature  mortality from non-communicable diseases between  twenty fifteen and twenty thirty is not likely to be met.
Policies  should also support the eradication of rheumatic  heart disease, which remains a persistent health  threat in the poorest countries.
Ambient air pollution and environmental lead expo sure remain serious health threats.
Effective health  systems and public health strategies exist to reduce  these risks.
Countries will need to adopt these stra tegies if they are to progress in achieving global goals  to reduce the burden of CVD.

Results The total cost for the SMC standalone campaign was USone hundred fifty-eight thousand, nine hundred thirty-four dollars, and the SMC VAS integration was USone hundred eighty-six thousand, four hundred twenty-six dollars.
Distribution and drug costs were the largest con tributors in the integrated and SMC-only campaign.
The SMC-only cost per child was  zero dollars.
Eighteen when eligible children received both SMC and VAS.
The integration  of VAS into the SMC campaign cycle incurred an additional UStwenty-seven thousand, four hundred ninety-two dollars over Cycle  one cost (USone hundred eighty-six thousand, four hundred twenty-six dollars – USone hundred fifty-eight thousand, nine hundred thirty-four dollars).
Fluctuations in distribution costs were the most  influential component of the cost per child.
Conclusion Integrating VAS with SMC campaigns increases the cost by USzero dollars.
Twenty-four per child, a modest increment considering the potential health benefits.
The results support the feasibility of this integration, in terms of cost, to combat child mortality from malaria  and malnutrition in Nigeria.
Further research is recommended to explore the cost-  effectiveness of this integrated distribution model.
Nutrition-related factors heighten the risk of all  cause childhood mortality [thirteen].
VAS is  cost effective in addressing global public health challenges among children [sixty-seven].
However, VAS coverage in Nigeria stands at forty-five.
Seasonal malaria  chemoprevention (SMC) can provide a ready platform for VAS delivery to enhance  coverage and access.

Additionally, incorporating administrative costs beyond the country  office of the implementing organization (i.
Malaria Consortium) in the costs would notably increase the total campaign  ten / thirteen PLOS One https://doi.org
Three hundred fifteen thousand, six hundred fifty-five October eight, twenty twenty-five cost.
The distinction was straightforward in first cycle, where  only SPAQ was administered.
Finally, the applicability of this analysis across different Nigerian  settings may be limited due to variability in supply and distribution costs.

Despite interventions such as insecticide‑treated nets  and indoor residual spraying, malaria prevalence remains high.
This study investigates this association using nationally representative data from the twenty twenty-one  Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey (NMIS).
Data on malaria prevention practices, household charac teristics, and children’s blood samples were collected.
The primary outcome was malaria test results (rapid diagnostic  test, RDT), with the type of toilet facility as the main predictor.

It remains  the leading cause of morbidity and mortality among  under-five children in sub-Saharan Africa [one].
In  sub-Saharan Africa, there were six hundred twenty-seven thousand malaria-related  deaths among children in twenty twenty, and an estimated two hundred forty-one mil lion new cases [two, three].
The largest prevalence is observed among chil dren between the ages of five and fifty-nine months (under-five) in  various geographic areas of the country [five].
Several studies have established a relationship between  housing structure and the risk of malaria infection in  Nigeria [six–eight].
Housing type/structure has been impli cated as an important risk factor for malaria infection  among under-five children in Nigeria [six–eight].
The likeli hood of contracting malaria is influenced by home design  [nine, ten].
Non-improved housing has been established as a  predictor of malaria infection among under-five children  [six, eight].
It becomes imperative as a major  issue of public health to look at this association.
Malaria  prevention strategies, including insecticide-treated nets and indoor spraying, have been effective over the years.
Despite this, malaria prevalence is still increasing.
The DHS provides standardized popu lation health and malaria-related data across develop ing countries.
Nigeria, located in West Africa,  bears the highest burden of malaria cases in sub-Saharan  Africa.
The dataset includes survey data from both urban  and rural areas, ensuring broad geographical representa tion, as illustrated in Fig.
A total of eighteen thirty-three children were  included in the dataset, with a weighted sample size of  one billion, seven hundred eighty-four million, eight hundred five thousand, four hundred eighty-six.
Malaria Journal Page three of eleven Fig.
Cases with missing, refused, or ambig uous malaria rapid test results were also excluded.
The twenty twenty-one NMIS used for this study was the third of its  kind, following earlier surveys conducted in twenty ten and twenty fifteen.
A two-stage  sampling method was employed to ensure national rep resentativeness.
This design ensured representa tion from all thirty-six states and the Federal Capital Territory  (FCT).
A total of five hundred sixty-eight clusters were identified, comprising  one hundred ninety-five urban and three hundred seventy-three rural areas [twelve].
During this process, global positioning system  (GPS) devices were used to record the coordinates of the  clusters [twelve].
In the second stage, a systematic sampling technique  was applied, with twenty-five households selected per cluster  using equal probability sampling.
Data collection for the  twenty twenty-one NMIS utilized computer-assisted personal inter viewing (CAPI) technology.
The  primary predictor variable, household sanitation facilities, was categorized based on the type of toilet facility used.
For analysis, flush  toilets were classified as improved sanitation, while pit  Asifat et al.
Malaria Journal Page four of eleven latrines without slabs, open defecation, and other forms  were categorized as unimproved sanitation [six].
The primary outcome variable, malaria infection,  was assessed using malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT)  results.
The original response options included nega tive, positive, not present, refused, or other.
Sociodemographic variables included  sex, wealth index, education level, and place of residence.
Sex was recorded as male or female and remained  unchanged.
Maternal education was classified as no educa tion, primary, secondary, or higher education, with cases  marked as "don’t know" excluded.
The place of residence  was categorized as urban or rural without modification.
Household construction materials were categorized into improved and unimproved based on quality and  durability.
Mosquito net  availability was assessed based on whether the household  had at least one designated sleeping net.
Statistical analysis T he outcome variable is the result of the malaria rapid  test, and the main predictor is the type of toilet facility.
Data was weighted according to DHS guidelines.
Vari ables were presented as frequencies and percentages.
The backward selection approach  was selected for the multivariate analysis, odd ratios and ninety-five percent confidence interval were reported with p-value  lesser than zero.
Five  All analyses were done with statistical software SAS ver sion nine.

This contrasts with previous studies in sub-Saharan Africa, such as the study by Yang et al.
[fifteen], which found that poor  sanitation and unsafe drinking water increased malaria  risk among children across multiple countries.
However,  broad regional analyses may not fully capture country specific variations in malaria transmission dynamics.
Instead, factors  such as poverty, rural residence, and maternal education  appear to play a more influential role.
Children from the poorest households had more than  three times the odds of malaria infection compared to  those from the richest households.
Similarly,  children whose mothers had no formal education were  at significantly higher risk than those whose mothers  attained higher education.
Many rural communities lack proper drainage, have open  water sources, and are surrounded by vegetation condu cive to mosquito proliferation.
Housing conditions were also significant, particularly  wall materials, with unimproved walls associated with an increased malaria risk.
However, unimproved roofing materials were  unexpectedly associated with a lower malaria risk.
Further  research is needed to explore these interactions.
A strong association was observed between mosquito  net usage and malaria risk.
This aligns with findings by Barker  et al.
[twenty-eight], which demonstrated that ITNs, particularly  those with dual active ingredients, significantly reduce  malaria transmission.
Expanding evidence-based strategies could enhance  malaria prevention and treatment efforts.
Socioeconomic  empowerment is crucial, as malaria disproportionately  affects low-income households.
Expanding programs like  Page seven of eleven Asifat et al.
Housing improvements and environmental manage ment are also essential.
Studies show that improved  housing structures with sealed walls, floors, and roofs  reduce malaria transmission by up to fifty percent [twenty-four].
Despite ITN distribution efforts, ensur ing proper and consistent use remains a challenge.

Similar initiatives in Nigeria could enhance ITN effec tiveness.
Finally, health education plays a crucial role.

T his study has several notable strengths that enhance  its credibility, reliability, and generalizability.
T he sample size and rigorous sampling methodology fur ther strengthen the study’s reliability.
Additionally, its com prehensive approach to categorizing environmental and  household factors strengthens its findings.
Despite its strengths, this study has several limita tions.
Partici pants may not have accurately reported their sanitation  conditions or net use, potentially affecting the observed  associations.
Second, the cross-sectional design of the survey used limits causal inference.
A longitudinal study design would provide stronger evidence of causal relationships.
Since data collec tion occurred at a single point in time, the findings may  not fully capture the seasonal burden of malaria.
Future  Asifat et al.
Malaria Journal Page nine of eleven research should incorporate seasonal adjustments for  a more comprehensive analysis.
Finally, there is potential for residual confounding.
Future studies should incorporate a more comprehensive set of con founders to strengthen the validity of findings.
Conclusion T his study provides critical insights into the determinants of malaria infection among under-five children in Nige ria.
T he study further underscores the importance of  mosquito prevention strategies, particularly the use of  insecticide-treated nets (ITNs).
Although ITN owner ship is widespread, ensuring consistent and proper use  remains a challenge.
Addressing these gaps through  targeted interventions can significantly reduce malaria  transmission.
First, efforts should focus on  improving housing conditions in rural and low-income  communities.
Infrastructure development should be integrated into malaria prevention programs to create healthier living environments.
Second, education plays a vital role in malaria con trol.
Public health campaigns should empha size not only ITN distribution but also effective use and  maintenance to maximize their protective benefits.
Addi tionally, routine net replacement programs should be  strengthened to ensure households have functional ITNs.
T hird, targeted malaria interventions should be  expanded in rural areas where the burden is highest.
Lastly, policy measures should integrate malaria con trol efforts with broader poverty alleviation programs.

Despite global efforts to control  the two diseases, their prevalence in high-risk regions like Nigeria remains  high.
Methods: The Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey (NMIS) twenty twenty-one dataset was used,  with a sample of ten thousand, one hundred twenty children aged six–fifty-nine months.
A two-stage sampling  method was applied.
Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests examined factors  associated with malaria and anemia prevalence.
Missing data were handled  using multiple imputations with chained equations (MICE).
Lastly, the adjusted  odds ratio was interpreted for the current study.
SAS was used in analyzing the  data and statistical significance was set at five percent significance level.
Results: The prevalence of malaria and anemia was thirty-six.
Sixty-six percent,  respectively, in children between six and fifty-nine months old in Nigeria.
The JGLMM  was used to examine malaria RDT and anemia findings in conjunction with  demographic, geographic, and socioeconomic covariates.
However, whether the mother knew of ways to prevent malaria was not  statistically significant regarding anemia.
Policymakers should prioritize mosquito net distribution  and healthcare access, particularly in rural areas.
The study’s novelty lies in  its handling of missing data through imputation techniques, enhancing the reliability of findings.

Despite the success of malaria reduction in Nigeria, some areas  still have a high prevalence of malaria parasitemia (five).
Anemia alone also affects over  fifty percent of individuals in the same population (six), making both illnesses  a great public health concern.
Malaria is more transmitted during the high temperature and  rainy seasons.
Malaria is not contagious.
However, it is possible to  contract the disease from another person through blood  transfusions or organ transplants (one, nine).
The WHO  African Region, with an estimated two hundred thirty-four million cases in twenty twenty-one,  accounted for about ninety-five percent of all cases (ten).

T he main objective of the current study is to determine the  malaria and anemia risk factors among children under five years of age  from Nigeria.
A two-stage sampling  strategy was adopted for the twenty twenty-one NMIS.
T he twenty twenty-one NIMS sample was stratified and selected in two stages.
Stratification was achieved by separating the thirty-six states and Federal  Capital Territory into urban and rural areas.
There were seventy-three sampling strata since there are no rural areas in Lagos.
Samples were selected independently in every stratum through a two-stage selection.
In the first stage, five hundred sixty-eight enumeration areas (EAs) were selected with  probability proportional to the EA size.
The EA size is the number of  households residing in the EA.
The sample selection was done in such  a way that it was representative of each state.
The result was five hundred sixty-eight  clusters throughout the country, one hundred ninety-five in urban areas, and three hundred seventy-three in rural  areas.
In the second stage’s selection, a fixed number of twenty-five households  Frontiers in Public Health two frontiersin.
One million, five hundred three thousand, eight hundred eighty-four were selected in every cluster through equal probability  systematic sampling.
T hree questionnaires were used in the twenty twenty-one NMIS: the Household  Questionnaire, the Woman’s Questionnaire, and the Biomarker Questionnaire (seven).
Based on The DHS Program’s model questionnaires,  the questionnaires were adapted to reflect the population and health  issues relevant to Nigeria.
After the questionnaires were finalized in  English, they were translated into Hausa, Yoruba, and Igbo (seven).
Using the DHS data from the twenty twenty-one NIMS, the children’s sample  was chosen using the household recode.
The data collection took place  from October to December twenty twenty-one.
Therefore, after applying the filter only to children between six–fifty-nine months old, the  sample used in this study became ten thousand, one hundred twenty (seven).
There were some missing  observations for some of the predictors, and a complete case analysis  was performed.
In the current study the power was calculated to  investigate if the sample selected will give adequate power to detect  the true effect of exposures.
Steptwo: calculated the mean and standard deviation, from the  three regions and found it to be three thousand, three hundred seventy-four and fourteen eighty.
Step three: Proc Power in SAS studio was used to calculate the power,  where the one sample means was adopted.
T he computed power was found to be  greater thanzero.
The section below outlines the imputation methods that  can be applied to missing data.
In the current study, children who were under five years old were  selected for analysis purposes.
Missing data It is usual to encounter missing data in epidemiological studies  (fourteen–sixteen).
Most survey data contain missing observations (seventeen), and  different methods can be employed to handle missing observations  (fifteen, seventeen).
The technique employed can affect the analysis outcome (fifteen).
T his could compromise the conclusion drawn from the results (eighteen).
In most cases, missing data is managed by dropping the cases that are  not fully measured (fifteen).
However, this study compared the complete  case and imputed data based on statistics of the standard error  resulting from the JGLMM joint model.
The comparison has been  thoroughly documented in the results section.
T he assumption was that the data was missing at random (MAR)  (seventeen).
When multiple imputation is applied to a, that is, the MAR  dataset and unbiased results with accurate estimates for the standard  error (SE) (nineteen).
In this study, multiple imputation by chained  equations was used.
Chained equations are also known as fully  conditional specification (FCS) (fifteen), and it is the algorithm adopted  by SAS Enterprise.
In this study, the FCS has  been employed for imputation using two iterations, with several  imputations (nimpute  equals to four).
Variables The current study considered two response variables.
The first one was malaria status for children under the age of five years.
The status of malaria was determined using RDT to check if the child had malaria (positive) or not (negative).
When  the hemoglobin concentration level adjusted for altitude is less than  eleven gram per decilitre (g/dL), the child is considered anemic, otherwise not anemic (thirteen, twenty-one).
In Nigeria, the studies that modeled anemia and malaria also used the same  independent variables found in the current study (five, eight).
However,  some variables were assumed to be associated with malaria and or  anemia in some parts of Africa (four, nine, thirteen).

Discussion In the current study, the power was calculated to check if the  selected sample will validate the ability to detect true associations.
The  value obtained for the power (Power  greater than zero.
The twenty twenty-one  Nigeria Indicator Malaria Indicator (NIMS) data create the sample.
T he joint generalized linear mixed model results were obtained from  SAS online University Edition.
The results from the covariance test  showed that there is a strong correlation between malaria and anemia  status.
The key factors obtained from the study  are divided into the following sections, which are environmental,  health-related, and socioeconomic.
This could result from  mosquitoes developing better in hot areas, which can be experienced  in areas with low altitudes (nine, twenty-seven).
The study revealed that children  who slept under a mosquito net the night before the survey had a  lower risk of having malaria and anemia.
This might be because  children who sleep under mosquito bed nets are being protected from  mosquito bites.
The result is consistent with what has been found in  previous studies, such as those by Gaston and Ramroop (nine).
The study  by Gayawan et al.
Health-related factors T he current study shows that malaria increases as the child grows,  and anemia decreases for the same group of children (thirteen).
Female children  are less likely to test positive for malaria using RDT and to have  anemia compared to male children.
One million, five hundred three thousand, eight hundred eighty-four opposite is true for anemia.
Therefore, this suggests that if the  environment is controlled for malaria, an effective reduction in  anemia will be observed (twenty-eight, twenty-nine).
The study further showed  that proper sanitation would significantly reduce malaria and anemia  in children from Nigeria.
However, children  from households with the main roof material thatch/palm leaf are less  likely to have anemia than those from households with wood.
This is  the only category that was statistically significant for anemia.
The  emphasis on education should not be taken for granted in countries  where there is a high prevalence of malaria or anemia.
Similar results were observed in the literature (four, nine, thirteen, twenty-five,  twenty-six, thirty).
This  result is consistent with what has been observed in a study by other studies in the literature (thirteen, thirty-three).
The inverse is also true; when malaria  reduces in children, so is anemia.
Conclusion T his study aimed to determine the risk factors associated with  positive malaria RDT results and anemia.
The current study used the  joint generalized linear mixed model.
The generalized linear mixed  models (GLMMs) effectively consider the fixed effects.
Furthermore,  the assumption of normality is relaxed (thirty-four), which is an advantage for  using the method in a survey dataset.
Thus, modeling the complete and  advantageous dataset results in a more accurate result.
However, whether the mother knows of ways to prevent malaria or not  did not have a statistically significant effect on anemia.
The findings also reveal that mothers’ education should  be encouraged and supported.
The  approach can be to educate caregivers on malaria risk factors and  some of the available ways to prevent malaria.
Furthermore, awareness  campaigns can be started through the radio or the media platforms  available to the wider community.
According to the NIMS twenty twenty-one report, it has been outlined that  about twenty-four percent of mosquito nets were not used the night before the survey.
This can be achieved through the  rolling out of mosquito nets and giving proper training on how to use  them for effective protection.

Future studies Longitudinal studies can be used to address the problem of  causality in future studies.
Even though each category has significant  risk factors: demographic, economic, and geographical.
Furthermore, the contributing factors to  anemia can be added to determine which ones add more significance to positive RDT results.
Therefore, a longitudinal study is suggested to address  this problem.

By twenty twenty-four, SMC  had been successfully implemented in all twenty-one eligible states in Nigeria.
Methods The study employed a pre-post plausibility evaluation design.
Results Data were collected in thirty-six health facilities: twelve each in Kogi state, Oyo state and the Federal Capital Territory.
The mean incidence of uncomplicated malaria was twenty cases per one thousand children aged three–fifty-nine months in twenty twenty-one, and nine  cases per one thousand children in twenty twenty-two.
The level of reduction varied  across the three study locations, with the greatest impact in Oyo state and no evidence of impact in Kogi state.
Incidence of all-cause fever per one thousand children was twenty-nine percent (ninety-five percent CI: fourteen–forty-one) lower in twenty twenty-two compared with twenty twenty-one.
Observed  levels of severe malaria and attributable deaths were too low to measure the impact of SMC on these secondary  outcomes.

Each year, malaria accounts for around two hundred fifty million  cases worldwide, with the African region accounting for  an estimated ninety-five percent of all cases [two, three].
Between two thousand and  twenty nineteen, malaria incidence declined in the region from three hundred sixty-eight  to two hundred twenty-two per one thousand population at risk.
However, an increase  to two hundred thirty-two per one thousand was reported in twenty twenty due to the disrup tions to health services during the COVID-nineteen pandemic  [four, five].
In Nigeria, it is estimated that malaria is responsi ble for approximately sixty percent of outpatient visits and thirty percent of  admissions [six].
It also contributes up to eleven percent of maternal  mortality, twenty-five percent of infant mortality, and thirty percent of under-five  mortality [seven, eight].
In twenty thirteen, WHO released an implementation guide  to help countries adopt and implement this new inter vention [twelve].
Following pilot studies in seven local gov ernment areas (LGAs) in three Sahelian states, Nigeria  adopted SMC as a chemoprevention strategy in twenty fourteen.
By twenty twenty, the intervention had been implemented across  all nine states that were targeted for the initial scale up phase.
T his led to the expansion of SMC to additional states.
As  of twenty twenty-four, SMC had been successfully implemented in all  twenty eligible states and the Federal Capital Territory, target ing about twenty million children.
Study setting T his study was conducted in three SMC implementing  locations: Oyo, Kogi and the Federal Capital Territory  Ikechukwu et al.

The FCT is located in the North Central geopoliti cal region in Nigeria and serves as the country’s capital.
It is situated within the savannah region with moderate  climatic conditions.
The peak of the rainy season in FCT  typically lasts from July and October.
Kogi state is situated  in north-central Nigeria within the tropical Guinean for est–savanna mosaic ecoregion.
The wet season occurs from April  to October.
The state also implements five SMC cycles  annually, beginning in May or June.

Discussion This study sought to evaluate the impact of SMC using  SPAQ to SMC eligible children aged three–fifty-nine months in  three study locations in Nigeria.

It is possible that this could  also reflect differences in the prevalence of resistance  markers associated with SP within the population.
Future research may explore the  Ikechukwu et al.
Malaria Journal Page ten of twelve influence of markers of SPAQ resistance on the level of  SMC effectiveness and impact in the region.
T he observable impact of SMC on the secondary out comes of interest, including all-cause fever, were less  clear.
Paradoxically, for FCT there was an increase in all-cause fever episodes  in twenty twenty-two compared to the previous year.
Consequently, the findings  may not fully capture the comprehensive level of pro tection offered by SMC in the study settings.
Like any study utilizing routine data sources, this study  has notable limitations.
This was due to the unavailability  of comparable control areas with similar epidemiological  Ikechukwu et al.
Concerns about  data quality limitations in routine data sources have been acknowledged previously.
Besides, it is likely that not all those who sought treat ment were primarily resident within the catchment areas  of the health facility.
Furthermore, of those who sought  care with symptoms suggestive of malaria, not all were  tested for parasitological confirmation.
These factors may  occur at different rates over time.
T hat has implications on the external validity and gener alizability of study findings.
Those adjustments might not have  completely accounted for other population dynamics  such as migration.
These limitations nonetheless present opportunities  for further HMIS data quality improvement and future  research efforts to consider.
As acknowledged earlier,  efforts are needed to strengthen facility-level and HMIS  data capture and reporting tools, methods and pro cesses.
Conclusion The study provides important and timely evidence on  the impact of SMC when delivered at scale under routine  programmatic conditions.

Malaria Journal Page two of twelve and accuracy of microscopy-based diagnosis.
One limitation of this study is the absence of comparative data  from other states in Nigeria where the interventions were not implemented.
Nigeria alone accounted for twenty-seven percent of malaria  cases globally and thirty-one percent of malaria-attributable deaths in  twenty twenty-two [three].
Approximately ninety-seven percent of Nigeria’s population is  at risk of malaria with children under five years (CUfive) and  pregnant women more susceptible [four].
Malaria microscopy and the use of Rapid Diagnostic  Test (RDTs) kits were approved as methods for testing  suspected malaria before treatment [six].
It improves  the overall management of patients with febrile illnesses  and may help reduce the emergence and spread of drug  resistance.
The malaria TPR is used to assess the effectiveness  of malaria interventions.
Further more, the ability to accurately conduct and interpret RDT  results continues to pose a challenge [seven].
This study aimed  to evaluate the impact of RDT cassette archiving and  BMMT on reducing malaria TPR.
Methods Study area T he study was carried out in Oyo State, located in South western Nigeria.
Known as the “Pace Setter state”.
Oyo  State has Ibadan as its capital city and comprises thirty-three Local  Government Areas (LGAs) classified into urban, semi urban, and rural (see Table one).
Oyo State has an esti mated population of approximately nine.
Five million people in  twenty twenty-two [one], primarily of the Yoruba ethnic group, alongside  minority groups like Hausa, Fulani, and Igbo.
Majority of  the population engages in agriculture, trading, and other  occupations, often residing in high-density urban areas.
Primary care: Involves primary health centres (PHCs)  and health posts providing essential services.
Study design A retrospective study of malaria data on DHIS two.
These  data were extracted from the health facilities’ National  Health Management Information System tools.
Malaria Journal Page four of twelve confirmation of malaria disaggregated for RDT and  microscopy.
Sampling technique All primary health facilities that reported malaria service  delivery data on DHIS two were included in the study.
Cassettes used are labelled with basic infor mation (patient name, date and time at start and end of  the test).
Results  are obtained after a certain number of minutes ranging  from fifteen–twenty min and following specific manufacturer’s  instructions [twenty-five].
The result indicates a positive test  when both the control and test lines are shown, while a  negative result will only show the control line.
Facility-based audits of archived RDT cassettes were conducted at the  seven hundred thirty-three PHFs.
In situations where  data misrepresentation was observed, disciplinary meas ures were meted out on the erring staff.
Data sets The malaria datasets for twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two for Oyo state  accessed from the DHIS two website were used in this  analysis.
Data was downloaded on sixth June twenty twenty-four from  the DHIStwo.
There was free access to the required data sets.
Fever is defined as axillary temperature of  greater than or  equals to thirty-seven.
Five at the time of visit to the health facility or reported experi ence of fever by clients within twenty-four h prior to presentation  at the health facility.
The average TPR was calculated for all the PHFs in the  state for each of the study months.
Data analysis A secondary data analysis was conducted for malaria data  extracted from DHIS two from January twenty twenty-one to Decem ber twenty twenty-two.

Malaria Journal SPSS version twenty-one was used to perform the analysis.
A  descriptive analysis of the data obtained was performed,  Frequency tables were used to show the distribution of  key socio-demographic variables.
Descriptive statistics  of percentage, frequency, mean, and standard deviation  were used to summarize the sociodemographic variables.
Considering the seasonal nature of malaria, a compari son of malaria data for the same period in twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two  was done.
An association was considered statistically  significant if the p-value was less than zero.
At the secondary health facilities, the average TPR  was reported across the seventeen selected SHFs.
Paired t-tests were performed to  compare the mean TPR for each period from January September twenty twenty-one and January –September twenty twenty-two.
At the PHCs, among patients with suspected malaria, eight hundred thirty-nine thousand, eight hundred thirty (ninety-nine percent)  had a diagnostic test performed, and of these, eight hundred twenty-one thousand, six hundred twenty-six  (ninety-seven.
Eight percent) were tested using RDT.
Overall, five hundred forty thousand, three hundred ninety-two (sixty-five.

Discussion Malaria transmission peaks during the rainy season, with  significant variations across different ecological zones in  the country [twenty-six].
Simi larly, malaria cases peaked in these months compared  to other months as shown in Table one.
Malaria RDT TPR  were almost similar between CUfive and persons ≥ five years  both in PHCs and secondary health facilities as seen in  this study.
Several studies have shown that malaria is more preva lent in rural areas compared to urban areas, hence often  described as a disease of the poor.
One study attributed  this difference to better living conditions and access to  healthcare facilities in urban areas [twenty-seven].
This study  also shows that in the two-year study period, test positivity  rate was highest in the rural LGAs and least in the semi urban LGAs.
The stratification lacked a clear distinc tion as factors that characterize very large urban settings  reducing malaria transmission intensity (e.
One Malaria RDT test positivity rate across primary health facilities from January twenty twenty-one–December twenty twenty-two Ayandipo et al.
Malaria Journal Page eight of twelve Fig.
Additionally, as this is an hospital-based study, the  incidence of malaria cannot be well elucidated.
These include inconsistent  data reporting, suboptimal use of diagnostic tools, and  gaps in healthcare worker training.
In this study, the average TPR was higher for RDT  (sixty-five percent) compared to microscopy (thirty-four percent).
This is similar to  what has been found in other studies [thirty-two].
Before the facility audits of RDT, a very high TPR  among febrile clients tested for malaria with RDT was  noted in the health facilities.
These figures, compared  to survey data, raise questions about the accuracy of  the routinely collected health facility data.
For instance,  data from Therapeutic Efficacy Study (TES) conducted  in Ibadan Oyo reported that the malaria incidence in  twenty twenty-one was forty-five.
Seven percent [thirty-four] compared to health facility test  positivity rates of seventy-one percent in the same year.
Field visits  often reveal inaccuracies in documentation and some times data falsification.
Malaria Journal provider’s cadre and previous training on other causes  of fever [thirty-five].
Some  studies have shown inflation of data or overreporting  of services provided, in addition to reclassification of  cases [thirty-five–thirty-seven].
This study showed improvement and a  reduction in the test positivity rate because of accurate  and improved data capture.
Prior to cassette archiv ing, this study revealed that the average reported TPR at  PHCs was seventy-seven percent, while it reduced to fifty-eight percent after archiving  commenced.
This is similar to the malaria TPR of fifty-five percent  reported in a twenty twenty-one hospital-based survey in Ibadan [eleven].
Malaria diagnosis using microscopy not only detects  Plasmodium species but also allows for speciation and  parasite density counting.
Training malaria micros copists significantly improves the accuracy of malaria  microscopy test results.
Following BMMT in Septem ber twenty twenty-one, the overall prevalence of malaria in this study  using microscopy was twenty-nine percent.
This study revealed a reduc tion in test positivity rates at the selected facilities after  the BMMT training.
Malaria Journal Page ten of twelve control efforts by reducing the number of false positive  test results.
This is particularly important in the context  of malaria elimination efforts, where accurate data is  critical for monitoring progress.
These measures would not only ensure the reliability of reported data  but also contribute to informed decision-making and  targeted interventions.
One limitation of this study is the  absence of comparative data from other states in Nigeria  where the interventions were not implemented.
This lack of comparison limits the ability to conclusively attribute  the observed improvements in TPR accuracy solely to the  interventions.
Conclusion The accuracy of reported data is another major concern  in the fight against malaria.
Factors contributing to data  inaccuracy include the reclassification of negative test  results as positive.
This practice not only skews malaria  prevalence statistics but also leads to the inappropriate  use of ACT, which can promote drug resistance.
The introduction of facility audits for RDTs has shown  promising results in improving data accuracy.
This study revealed a significant reduction in the test positivity rate  after the implementation of cassette archiving and audits.
Similar improve ments were noted in accuracy of reports from malaria  microscopy following the basic malaria microscopy  training.
Improving the accuracy of malaria diagnosis is criti cal for effective health service planning and achiev ing malaria control targets.
Continued investment in training, infrastructure, and  regular audits will help address the challenges faced in  malaria diagnosis.
Accurate data is essential for meas uring progress, making informed decisions, and ulti mately reducing the burden of malaria in Nigeria.
By addressing these challenges, Nigeria can make signifi cant strides towards better health outcomes and con trol of malaria.
The authors also appreciate all the  health workers in Oyo for always doing their best to report accurate data in a  timely manner.
The efforts and time taken by the reviewers  assigned to review this paper by the journal are also appreciated.

This study aimed to determine the prevalence and factors associated  with malaria and anaemia among children aged two–eighteen months in Osun State.
Methods A cross-sectional household malariometric study was conducted in eighty communities across eight Local Gov ernment areas (LGAs) in Osun State.
Ethical approval was obtained from Osun State Health Research Ethical Committee  (OSHREC/PRS/five hundred sixty-nineTthree hundred twelve/ on the twenty-second of May twenty twenty-three.
Malaria test positivity was determined by rapid diagnostic test (RDT)  and microscopy.
In addition, haemoglobin levels were measured using Haemocue® Hb two hundred one.
Caregivers were interviewed  on malaria management practices using tools adapted from Nigeria Malaria Indicator Survey.
Results A total of four hundred children aged two–eighteen months were assessed in this study, which was conducted  in July twenty twenty-three.

Conclusion Malaria infection and anaemia were found to be higher in older children.
Household wealth and child’s  age were significantly associated with malaria infection.
These findings would inform the positioning of PMC interven tion touch-points to reduce malaria burden in young children.
It is the primary cause of morbidity  and mortality for this age group, with over ninety-five thousand deaths  from malaria annually [two].
In addition, there are ongoing efforts to pro vide evidence for the implementation of perennial malaria  chemoprevention (PMC) [five].
The children at high-risk of malaria infection can be  given antimalarial medicines at predefined intervals to  prevent transmission.
The strategy recommends using expanded  programme on immunization (EPI) as the platform for  delivering PMC.
To support decision-making at the  country level, PMC recommendation must be accompa nied by available research evidence.
The WHO encourages acquisition of evidence in the local context, before  national malaria programmes’ adoption, adaptation and  scale-up [six].
Women of reproductive age (fifteen–forty-nine years)  were interviewed and their children aged two–eighteen months  recruited for biomarker testing.

Four hundred (four hundred) children  were randomly selected across eighty clusters/communities (five (five) from each cluster/community) in eight LGAs.
T he data collectors mobilized the eligible children from  selected households, to a designated centre within  the community.
At this centre, a team of laboratory  scientists collected blood samples from the children.
One child was randomly selected  per household.
The five (five) children sampled from each  cluster/community were tested for malaria and anaemia.
Study population(s) questionnaire T hree questionnaires were utilized based on the study  objectives.
These include name, sex, age, residency  status, and line number.
The respondent to this questionnaire  was usually the head of the household.
In addition, the household  questionnaire collected information on ownership  and use of bed nets.
All women aged fifteen–forty-nine years  identified in the household were interviewed.
Child questionnaire captured basic information  about every child selected for the study.
Information  such as age, sex, history of fever, malaria, hospital  admission due to malaria amongst others were  captured.
A pre-and post-test was conducted to  analyse the training impact.

Data collection The data collection was conducted July twenty twenty-three.
In addition, sociodemographic and clinical information were  captured for all children that were randomly selected.
This included their age, sex, height, weight, temperature,  haemoglobin concentration, positive or negative malaria  test results by RDT.
Blood samples were collected from all  eligible children whose caregivers gave written informed  consent.
Histidine-Rich  Protein two (HRPtwo) RDT was conducted according to  manufacturer’s manual and blood spotted on the filter  paper according to the SOP.
The filter papers were air  dried and stored individually in plastic sleeves with seal locks with desiccant sachets.
These blood spot samples  are currently stored at room temperature away from  extreme light and heat for future parasite genotyping  assays (NGS).
Haemoglobin concentration assessed with  concentration  lesser than seven.
Zero g/dl and those with malaria infection  were referred to the nearest health facility for treatment  [nine].
Thin films of duplicate blood slides for microscopy  were fixed and the films stained with three percent Giemsa for one h.
Data management and statistical analysis T he household wealth tertile was computed using the  principal components analysis (PCA) technique.
Then, the factor loadings and z-scores were calculated.
For each  household, the indicator values were multiplied by the  loadings and summed to produce the household’s wealth  index value.
The standardized z-score was used to classify  the overall scores to wealth tertile (poor, medium, rich).
Data was collected and entered into Microsoft Excel and  exported to Stata Version sixteen (StataCorp; College Station,  TX, USA) for further analysis.
Counts, percentage and descriptive statistics were used for univariate estimates.
The prevalence of malaria parasites was expressed in  percentage.
For bivariate analysis, Chi-square test was  used.
The variable(s) statistically significant at p  lesser than zero.
Five were included in the multivariable logistic regression.
A multivariable logistic regression analysis was used to  examine the factors associated with malaria infection  among children aged two–eighteen months.
Laboratory analysis Malaria microscopy slides were stained in the field and  later read in the NIMR laboratory.
The microscopy results  such as detection, species, stage, gametocyte detection,  asexual parasite count, gametocyte count were included.
During data analysis, the children household data were  linked by the unique identifier to the samples collected  for malariometric assessment.
The slides were examined  at a magnification of a one thousand X binocular light microscope  and the parasites counted [ten].
Slides were considered negative if no parasite was detected  after reading two hundred high-powered fields.
The presence  of gametocytes was also recorded.
Thin blood smears  were reviewed for non P. falciparum infections.
Two  microscopists read all slides independently, and parasite  densities were calculated by averaging the two counts.
Definition of anaemia Haemoglobin levels were calculated to determine the  anaemia status.
A Hb reading of Hb  lesser than seven.

Discussion The findings from this study showed malaria prevalence  by microscopy was highest (fifteen.
Zero percent) among children  seven–twelve months, while by RDT, it was highest (forty-eight.
Zero percent) among children thirteen–eighteen months.
The prevalence of malaria  by RDT is similar to the report observed amongst febrile  patients in Iwo, a community also in Osun State [thirteen].
It was however higher than the result obtained for Osun  state in the twenty twenty-one NMIS [fourteen].
Though malaria prevalence  dropped from forty-two percent in twenty ten to twenty-one.
There was a shift of  medical resources from malaria control to emergency COVID-nineteen response during the pandemic.
This caused  disruptions, reductions, and delays in malaria prevention  and control interventions.
By implication, malaria prevention and control  interventions must be sustained to prevent resurgence.
Other prevalence surveys reported in the South West  region of Nigeria among under-five using microscopy  was seventy-nine.

Study implications, direction of future research  and limitations This study has critical implications for public health.
